events.title: ASG bill targets pests in the dorms
events.body: ASG introduced a bill calling for a ban on bugs in residence halls; the Herald's editorial cartoon depicted a cockroach imperiled by the resolution. The paper's editorial page separately argued the university's protective inspection policy was unnecessary.

events.title: ASG re-endorses dorm inspections after nearly missing the vote
events.body: ASG voted to re-endorse dormitory room inspections, in a session the Herald reported the government had nearly slept through. The same issue covered ASG's sponsorship of an international film and dance series and an attorney's interest in a dorm inspection case.

events.title: ASG bill proposes a stricter room-entry rule
events.body: ASG introduced a bill proposing a stricter rule governing staff entry into student rooms, continuing the fall's running fight over dormitory inspections.

events.title: Resolution 80-32 asks for change machines in the dorms
events.body: ASG passed Resolution 80-32, requesting that change machines be installed in residence halls.

organization.note: Mark Wilson and Greg Zoeller were elected to other top ASG offices in the same April 1980 election; the Herald index does not specify which.

leaders.name: Marcell Bush
leaders.note: Herald bylines consistently spell this "Marcel Bush" (one L); the plaque and this site list "Marcell Bush" - spelling unverified. Resigned the ASG presidency 14 January 1982; David Payne succeeded him for the balance of the term.
profile: Marcel Bush won the Associated Student Government presidency in April 1981, defeating David Sturgeon after a campaign the Herald said saw candidates "playing big time politics." Close races elsewhere on the ballot prompted recounts.

In office that fall, ASG raised its own campaign spending limit and vetoed a plan to pay an education lobbyist, days after rallying publicly for higher education funding. Bush later listed the fall rally as one achievement of his term.

Bush resigned the presidency on or shortly before 14 January 1982, reported the same week as the retrospective on his term. David Payne succeeded him; Board of Regents minutes from 30 January 1982 name Payne the new SGA president.

leaders.name: David Payne
leaders.note: Plaque reads 1982; this site originally filed him under 1982-83. Board of Regents minutes (30 Jan 1982) and Herald coverage place him as SGA president succeeding Marcel Bush, who resigned 14 Jan 1982, filling the balance of the 1981-82 term. Margaret Ragan, elected president in April 1982, led the separate 1982-83 term - the two are not the same office-year.

sources.label: WKU Board of Regents minutes, 30 Jan 1982

profile: David Payne first appears in the indexed record in February 1981 with a Herald letter titled 'Apathy Erased.' By October 1981, before he held the presidency, he was writing on the Associated Student Government's behalf, declaring that ASG was rallying for higher education as budget cuts loomed.

Payne became ASG's president after Marcel Bush resigned on 14 January 1982; Board of Regents minutes from the January 30 meeting name him the new SGA president. In early February the Herald reported that Payne wanted another adviser for ASG, and its editorial page attacked his judgment, while a report the next week said Payne considered certain resolutions misdirected.

Later that month, letter writers to the Herald argued that Payne had been made a victim in the affair; the indexed headline does not state what precipitated it. His name does not appear in the indexed headlines of the April 1982 election that chose Margaret Ragan for the 1982-83 term, nor in the 1982-83 issues examined - consistent with his presidency ending with Bush's original term.

events.title: Sandra Norfleet elected student regent
events.body: Reported by Kevin Francke. The same issue has a group set to speak on the Associated Student Government's behalf and Western's 1982 budget coming off hold.

events.title: ASG announces its goals for the year
events.body: The Associated Student Government announced its goals for the coming year. Within two weeks its executives were defending their actions in the Herald, whose editorial page complained that petty politics plagued the organization.

events.title: Campaign spending limit raised
events.body: ASG voted to increase its campaign spending limit. The change followed a week of debate over whether the cap should rise.

events.title: ASG vetoes plan to pay an education lobbyist
events.body: The Associated Student Government vetoed a plan to pay an education lobbyist. The vote came weeks after ASG had rallied publicly for higher education funding.

events.title: ASG appoints a council to decide disputes
events.body: ASG appointed a council to decide internal disputes. The same issue reported that the regents bill, changing how the student regent was chosen, had passed the state House.

events.title: Five students seek the student regent seat
events.body: Five students sought the student regent spot in the first campus-wide election for the seat. The February 9 vote produced no majority, forcing a runoff the following week.

events.title: Ragan and Sargent survive the presidential primary
events.body: Margaret Ragan and Glenn Sargent survived the Associated Student Government presidential primary. The field had included Jack Smith, Kerrie Stewart and Jack Murphree, whose supporters filled the Herald's letters pages.

events.title: General election results voided
events.body: The student government election results were voided, a decision the Herald said disgusted the candidates. A repeat general election was scheduled for April 20.

events.title: Margaret Ragan wins the repeated election
events.body: Margaret Ragan won the ASG presidency in the repeated general election. The new officers were sworn in the following week.

events.title: ASG president Marcel Bush resigns
events.body: Associated Student Government president Marcel Bush resigned. The same issue reported him listing the fall's higher-education rally as one achievement of his term.

events.title: Board of Regents minutes name David Payne the new SGA president
events.body: Minutes of the WKU Board of Regents meeting identified David Payne as the new Student Government Association president, confirming his succession after Marcel Bush's resignation.

src.label: WKU Board of Regents minutes, 30 Jan 1982

events.title: Payne asks for a second ASG adviser
events.body: President David Payne said the Associated Student Government wanted another adviser. The Herald's editorial page criticized his judgment the same week.

executive.name: Marcel Bush
executive.note: Resigned 14 Jan 1982.

executive.name: David Payne
executive.note: Succeeded Bush; named in Board of Regents minutes 30 Jan 1982.

src.label: WKU Board of Regents minutes, 30 Jan 1982

leaders.name: Sandra Norfleet
leaders.note: Student regent, not president. Election reported in the Herald, 18 February 1982.
profile: No candidate won a majority on February 9, forcing a runoff, which Norfleet won on February 16. The Herald reported her election as student regent in its February 18 issue.

Her initial term was short: by mid-April 1982 the Herald noted that the student regent's 2-month term was nearing its end. She is listed among the 1982-83 student leaders, and in February 1983 the Herald's editorial page was still weighing the office, insisting the student regent must represent everyone.

leaders.name: Margaret Ragan
leaders.note: Confirmed by her own byline in the Herald, 3 Feb 1983 ('Ragan, Margaret. Associated Student Government, Student Regent Position Separate'), plus the primary and election-night headlines in the same spring.
profile: Margaret Ragan survived the April 1982 Associated Student Government presidential primary along with Glenn Sargent, emerging from a five-way field. Endorsement letters for her ran in the Herald through both rounds of the election.
After the first general election was voided, Ragan won the presidency in the repeated election held April 20, 1982. She and the other new officers were sworn in before the month was out.

Midway through her term Ragan used the Herald's pages to explain that the ASG presidency and the student regent seat were now separate positions. Her spring saw a grade plan, a student shuttle vote, and a contested rewrite of the ASG constitution before Jack Smith was elected to succeed her.

events.title: Norfleet wins the student regent runoff
events.body: No candidate won a majority in the February 9 student regent primary, forcing a runoff. Sandra Norfleet won the runoff on February 16.

events.title: Ragan and Sargent survive the ASG primary
events.body: Margaret Ragan and Glenn Sargent survived the Associated Student Government presidential primary, emerging from a five-way field.

events.title: Norfleet's short regent term nears its end
events.body: The Herald noted that the student regent's two-month term was already nearing its end, a reminder of how short a stopgap the office had been.

events.title: Ragan wins the presidency in a repeated election
events.body: The first general election was voided, and Margaret Ragan won the Associated Student Government presidency in the repeated election held April 20. She and the other new officers were sworn in before the month was out.

events.title: ASG floats a shuttle service, and Ragan explains the split with the regent seat
events.body: The same issue that carried President Margaret Ragan's Herald piece explaining that the ASG presidency and student regent seat were now separate positions also reported ASG was considering a shuttle service, the proposal put to a student vote the following week.

events.title: Grade plan passes; students vote for a shuttle
events.body: ASG passed a grade plan, and 206 students voted for a campus shuttle service.

events.title: Constitution changes approved; filing opens
events.body: The Associated Student Government approved changes to its constitution, and ten students filed for offices ahead of the deadline. Dean Charles Keown publicly questioned the revisions the following week, as filings swelled to 68.

events.title: 500 vote in the ASG primary
events.body: About 500 students voted in the Associated Student Government primary. The Herald's letters pages carried a steady stream of endorsements for presidential candidate Jack Smith.

events.title: Jack Smith wins the ASG presidency
events.body: Jack Smith won the presidency of the Associated Student Government, and students voted for the ASG constitutional revisions on the same ballot. The Herald had dared students to vote at all in a sardonic election day editorial.

events.title: 24 elected to Senate
events.body: Twenty-four students were elected to the Associated Student Government Senate, the same issue reporting increased dormitory hours had been proposed.

events.title: ASG endorses a $15 athletic fee
events.body: The outgoing congress endorsed a $15 athletic fee. The vote came as the Board of Regents turned its focus to the budget.

executive.name: Margaret Ragan
executive.note: Won a repeated general election 20 April 1982 after the first was voided; succeeded by Jack Smith in April 1983.

executive.name: Sandra Norfleet
executive.note: Separately elected office; her term ran only from mid-February to roughly mid-April 1982, a two-month stopgap before the 1982-83 cycle.

senate.note: Twenty-four senators were elected 1 March 1983; the Herald did not name a Speaker or list committees in the coverage found so far.

leaders.name: Jack Smith
leaders.note: Two-year plate. Confirmed by name in Herald headlines across his whole term, from the April 1983 win through the April 1985 retrospective on his presidency ending.
profile: Jack Smith first ran for the Associated Student Government presidency in spring 1982, drawing repeated endorsement letters in the Herald, and though Margaret Ragan won that race, Smith and Lonnie Sears took awards as the year closed. He returned as a candidate in March 1983, when 68 students filed for ASG positions and his supporters again filled the letters pages.

Smith won the presidency of the Associated Student Government in the April 12, 1983 election, in which students also approved constitutional revisions. His victory came after roughly 500 students had voted in the primary the week before.

His presidency was colorful and contentious: the fall brought a discount card controversy, letters accusing him of partying while committees waited and others defending him, and a December cartoon that he wrote in to protest. In April 1984 the Herald caught him impersonating a bunny as his ASG ran a low-turnout poll on beer and a campus pub.

Smith's plaque term runs two years, 1983-85, and the Herald's own account of his exit backs that up: its April 11, 1985 issue reported him ending his term as ASG president in an article headlined 'Jack Smith Ends Term as Associated Student Government President,' alongside a companion piece crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in the organization.

events.title: Escort service returns; discount card floated
events.body: The Herald's opening issue reported that the student escort service would resume and that ASG might sponsor a discount card. Filing for freshman elections was set to begin September 19.

events.title: Discount card plan draws fire
events.body: ASG voted to study the discount card after the Herald editorialized that the organization should govern, not market cards. A week later the paper reported ASG would offer members a commission on card sales, prompting letters calling the plan cheap shots and old tricks.

events.title: ASG passes incomplete-grade deadline proposal
events.body: The Associated Student Government passed its proposal on the deadline for incomplete grades, after tabling it the week before. The grade issue had occupied ASG since September.

events.title: ASG voids its own procedures amid growth
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG voided its own procedures, while also noting growth in membership and a congress weighing 14 proposals. The editorial page mocked the body with a cartoon, and Jack Smith wrote in to say the cartoon aggravated him.

events.title: Student legislature may rejoin ASG
events.body: The Kentucky Student Legislature delegation was reported possibly rejoining the Associated Student Government. Letter writers sparred the same day over whether the ASG stereotype was deserved.

events.title: Top four ASG offices decided without runoffs
events.body: The top four Associated Student Government spots were decided, the Herald reported, as ASG emphasized representation. About 450 students had voted in the primary the week before.

events.title: ASG polls students on beer and a campus pub
events.body: ASG began a student poll on the beer and campus pub issue on general election day. The Herald's editorial page argued the economics of the campus pub plan were faulty.

events.title: Low turnout may force a beer poll revote
events.body: Low turnout threatened to spur a revote in the ASG beer poll. The same issue reported president Jack Smith impersonating a bunny for the season.

events.title: ASG election day: candidates court votes for the top offices
events.body: The Herald urged students to the polls for the Associated Student Government election. Beyond the presidential contest, candidates for ASG's other top offices - including Bob Shults, Laura McClellan, Traci Turner, Kim Binkley and Allan Kujala - each drew endorsement letters in the paper; the Herald index does not specify which office each sought.

organization.note: Bob Shults, Laura McClellan, Traci Turner, Kim Binkley and Allan Kujala all appear as candidates for ASG's top offices in the April 1983 election coverage; the Herald index does not specify which offices they sought or who won them.

leaders.name: Jack Smith
leaders.note: Two-year plate. Either re-elected or the plaque compresses two terms.
profile: Smith presided over a productive opening to the 1984-85 year. By the third week of September the Herald reported that four ASG proposals had been made reality, and the congress had begun studying a student book exchange, which became the signature project of his final year.
By mid-year the record was mixed. The book exchange venture appeared likely to take a summer pause, and the organization was weighing whether to fight cuts to education funding.

His term ended in April 1985. The Herald covered his exit with a news story headlined that Smith was ending his term as ASG president, an editorial crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in the organization, and an editorial cartoon. The SGA plaque records him on a two-year 1983-85 plate.

events.title: Apathy as an editorial cartoon
events.body: 'Voter Apathy Can be Solved' ran alongside a cartoon on election apathy and a report that a 24-hour open house was under discussion.

events.title: Four proposals made reality in the third week of class
events.body: The Herald reported that four Associated Student Government proposals had already been carried out, and that the congress was beginning a study of a student book exchange. The exchange went on to become the running project of the year.

events.title: The grade scale proposal is denied
events.body: ASG's proposal for a new grade scale was denied, one week after the congress's early run of successes. It was the first setback of the fall reported in the Herald's coverage.

events.title: ASG wants less general education
events.body: The congress went on record wanting a reduction in general education requirements. It was an early instance of the body intervening in curriculum policy, three years before the fights over the General Education Task Force.

events.title: LaMont Jones drops out of a revote
events.body: LaMont Jones withdrew from an ASG revote, and the same issue carried an editorial cartoon on the organization. A disputed election requiring a revote marked the low point of the fall semester.

events.title: Education cuts loom and the book exchange stalls
events.body: ASG weighed a fight against state education cuts, while its book exchange venture looked likely to pause for the summer. Both stories ran in the same late-January issue.

events.title: Four file for congress president
events.body: A fourth candidate filed for ASG congress president and a debate was set, as the spring filing period opened. The same issue carried letters both applauding an ASG bill and requesting its support.

events.title: McKinney and Watkins take the primary
events.body: Mitchell McKinney and Chris Watkins rode their experience to victory in the ASG primary. The congress also passed a resolution on grade point averages the same week.

events.title: Jack Smith ends his term
events.body: The Herald marked the end of Jack Smith's presidency with a news story, an editorial crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in ASG, and an editorial cartoon. Mitchell McKinney had been elected the new president the week before.

leaders.name: Mitchell McKinney
leaders.note: Named explicitly as SGA president in the outgoing congress's own commendation bill, Bill 86-13-S (3 Apr 1986), which settles the name.

sources.label: SGA Bill 86-13-S, Commendation of President, 3 Apr 1986

profile: Before he was a candidate, McKinney wrote a Herald op-ed on 21 March 1985 headlined 'Associated Student Government Shouldn't Force Bill,' one of a pair of dueling pieces the paper ran on the same question - a sign he was already active in ASG's legislative debates a week before he entered the presidential race.

McKinney won the spring 1985 primary on a ticket with Chris Watkins on March 28, the Herald's headline saying the pair rode experience to their primary victory over a field that included candidate Stan Reagan. He was announced as the new Associated Student Government president in the Herald of April 4, in the same issue that reported an unnamed legislative group rejoining ASG. The record found so far does not confirm what office, if any, Watkins went on to hold.

In office, the congress abolished its own Finance Committee that September and, the following spring, wrote a Financial Advisory Council into the ASG bylaws in its place. The spring 1986 session was especially active: bills created major/minor college representative seats, revised the membership application process, asked Board of Regents members to attend an SGA meeting, sought chains for Pearce-Ford Tower windows, and pushed for a welcome sign at Normal Drive and University Boulevard.

In March 1986 McKinney pulled out of the race for a second term. The same issue carried a piece arguing that student government needed a strong leader, and the field he left behind grew to four candidates before Tim Todd won the presidency that April. The outgoing congress commended McKinney's work in Bill 86-13-S on April 3, and the WKU Board of Regents included a resolution honoring him, alongside outgoing president John D. Minton, at its meeting of August 8, 1986. A 1986 presidential proclamation he signed honoring English professor Thomas Jones survives in the SGA records.

events.title: An apathy editorial greets a 24-hour open house debate
events.body: The Herald ran an apathy editorial and cartoon aimed at student government alongside a report on debate over 24-hour open house policy in the dorms.

events.title: Dueling op-eds spar over forcing a bill
events.body: The Herald ran a pair of opposing opinion pieces, both headlined "Associated Student Government Shouldn't Force Bill," one by future ASG president Mitchell McKinney and the other by Jamie Morton.

events.title: McKinney and Watkins win the ASG primary
events.body: Mitchell McKinney and Chris Watkins won the Associated Student Government presidential primary over a field that included candidate Stan Reagan.

events.title: McKinney elected president; a legislative group rejoins ASG
events.body: Mitchell McKinney was elected Associated Student Government president. The same issue reported that an unnamed legislative group had rejoined ASG.

events.title: ASG abolishes its Finance Committee
events.body: The congress voted to abolish its own Finance Committee, a structural change later reversed in part when a Financial Advisory Council was written into the bylaws the following spring.

src.label: SGA Bill 85-1-F, Abolishment of Finance Committee

events.title: ASG orders its own student discount card
events.body: The congress passed legislation calling for ASG to produce its own student discount card, one of several consumer-service ideas the group pursued that fall.

src.label: SGA Bill 85-15-F, Production of Own Student Discount Card

events.title: A 20-vote margin and a GPA debate
events.body: About 20 votes separated the top two finishers in a fall ASG election, and the congress debated setting a grade-point average requirement for its own members. Both stories ran in the same late-October issue.

events.title: Alcohol on campus studied again
events.body: ASG returned to the question of alcohol on campus, an issue that had already produced a student poll and a campus pub debate in 1984. The congress opened a new study of the policy.

events.title: A shuttle to the mall
events.body: The congress discussed running a shuttle service from campus to the mall. It was one of several consumer-service ideas, alongside student discount cards, floated that fall.

events.title: Lighting proposal defeated
events.body: Student government defeated a campus lighting proposal in the last week of the fall semester. It was one of the few outright defeats of legislation reported that year.

events.title: Fall-break bill narrowly passes
events.body: A bill calling for a fall break narrowly passed ASG. The proposal drew an opposing editorial in the next issue calling the extra break impractical and not needed.

events.title: No day off for Martin Luther King Day
events.body: ASG rejected a proposal to dismiss classes for the Martin Luther King holiday, one week after passing the fall-break bill. The King holiday question returned to the congress the following year.

events.title: McKinney withdraws from re-election
events.body: Mitchell McKinney pulled out of the race for a second term as ASG president. The same issue carried a piece arguing that student government needed a strong leader.

events.title: Library hours proposals, and elections delayed a week
events.body: ASG proposals asked for more library hours, and the spring elections were pushed back a week. The same issue carried dueling letters on whether the organization was in trouble.

events.title: College representative seats created
events.body: The congress created major/minor college representative seats within its own membership.

src.label: SGA Bill 86-19-S, Voting of Representatives for Colleges

events.title: ASG revises its membership application
events.body: The congress adopted a revised application process for SGA membership.

src.label: SGA Bill 86-21-S, Adoption of New Application

events.title: ASG asks regents to attend a meeting
events.body: The congress asked that Board of Regents members attend and speak at one SGA meeting during their term.

src.label: SGA Bill 86-22-S, Attendance of Regents at Meetings

events.title: ASG seeks chains for Pearce-Ford Tower windows
events.body: The congress asked for chains to be placed on Pearce-Ford Tower windows so they could be opened.

src.label: SGA Bill 86-26-S, Placing of Chain on Windows

events.title: Financial Advisory Council written into the bylaws
events.body: The congress incorporated the Financial Advisory Council into the ASG bylaws, months after abolishing its own Finance Committee.

src.label: SGA Bill 86-3-S, Incorporation of Councils into By-Laws

events.title: Outgoing congress commends President McKinney
events.body: The outgoing congress passed a bill commending the work of SGA president Mitchell McKinney as his term ended.

events.title: Pranks and accusations mar the races
events.body: The Herald reported that pranks and accusations had marred the ASG races, and printed the election results in the same issue. Tim Todd emerged from the field as the new president.

events.title: ASG pushes for a campus welcome sign
events.body: The congress pushed for a welcome sign to be placed at the intersection of Normal Drive and University Boulevard.

src.label: SGA Bill 86-36-S, Placing of Welcome Sign on Campus

events.title: ASG commends outgoing President Minton
events.body: The congress passed a bill commending outgoing WKU president John D. Minton for his service to the university.

src.label: SGA Bill 86-39-S, Commendation of Dr. John D. Minton

events.title: Regents honor McKinney at term's end
events.body: The WKU Board of Regents included a resolution honoring outgoing ASG president Mitchell McKinney, alongside honors for Georgia Bates and outgoing WKU president John Minton, at its August meeting - held the same day Kern Alexander was named the university's new president.

executive.name: Mitchell McKinney
executive.note: Ran on a primary ticket with Chris Watkins in spring 1985; the record found so far does not confirm what office, if any, Watkins held afterward. Withdrew from re-election in March 1986 and was commended by the outgoing congress that April.

committees.name: Finance Committee
committees.note: Abolished by the congress in September 1985.

committees.name: Financial Advisory Council
committees.note: Written into the ASG bylaws in April 1986, replacing the abolished Finance Committee.

senate.note: Spring 1986 also created major/minor college representative seats (Bill 86-19-S) and revised the SGA membership application process (Bill 86-21-S).

leaders.name: Timothy Todd
leaders.note: Two-year plate. A 1987 Herald piece reports a candidate shortage and mentions a Tim Todd race.
profile: Todd reached the April 1986 runoff against Greg Elder after Mitchell McKinney's withdrawal left the presidential field open. The Herald reported the two-man race on 3 April, with the general election the following week.

Days after an election week the Herald described as marred by pranks and accusations, the paper identified Todd as the new ASG president in a sharply critical opinion piece headlined that he lacked knowledge of his own issues. Todd answered in print the following issue, criticizing the paper's reporting.
His first fall opened with an approved budget of $12,100, a plan to reach students by phone for their ideas and needs, and an ASG retreat featuring university president Kern Alexander.

events.title: Twenty years of amendments consolidated into one document
events.body: The constitution of the WKU Associated Students with amendments - the only surviving snapshot of how the 1966 framework had been patched over two decades. A Judicial Council roster for 1986-87 survives alongside it.

events.title: A $12,100 budget and a retreat with the university president
events.body: ASG approved a $12,100 budget, planned a phone outreach effort to hear students' ideas and needs, and announced a retreat featuring university president Kern Alexander. All three stories ran in the second week of the fall semester.

events.title: A minor change in voting
events.body: ASG sought a minor change in its voting procedures early in the fall term. It was the first structural tinkering of the Todd presidency.

events.title: Rules suspended, bills passed
events.body: The congress suspended its rules to pass a batch of bills in a single meeting. The rush came as the spring filing period for elections was opening.

events.title: Martin Luther King bill splits the congress
events.body: A Martin Luther King bill passed the congress with members split by the argument, a year after ASG had rejected dismissing classes for the holiday. The same issue reported that Tim Todd and Greg Elder would battle again for the presidency.

events.title: Attendance drops after the speeches
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG attendance fell off once campaign speeches had been heard. An accompanying piece warned voters that talk was cheap in the presidential race.

events.title: An amendment dies of low member turnout
events.body: A constitutional amendment was defeated because too few members turned up to vote on it. The failure came in the same week as the presidential election.

events.title: The Herald calls the race for Elder; the index calls it no contest
events.body: On election day the Herald endorsed challenger Greg Elder as the better choice to lead ASG, ran a letter calling the organization impotent, and headlined the race itself as no contest. The indexed issues that survive do not record the published result; the SGA plaque carries Todd through 1988 on a two-year plate.

leaders.name: Timothy Todd
leaders.note: Two-year plate. A 1987 Herald piece reports a candidate shortage and mentions a Tim Todd race.
profile: Todd sought a second term in spring 1987 in a rematch against Greg Elder, the man he had beaten the year before. The Herald reported the two would battle again in its 19 March issue.

On election day the Herald endorsed Elder as the better choice and indexed the race itself under the headline no contest. The surviving indexed issues do not record the published result; the SGA plaque lists Todd on a single 1986-88 plate, and no other president appears in the 1987-88 record.
The 1987-88 year under the two-year plate ended with the election of Scott Whitehouse on 7 April 1988, closing out the era of the Todd presidency.

events.title: Not enough candidates to fill the ballot
events.body: ASG races faced a candidate shortage; one report notes a candidate entered a race to help a rival rather than to win. The same issue has ASG tabling a phone bill after amendment.

events.title: Dropping the intercollegiate legislature considered
events.body: ASG considered dropping its membership in the intercollegiate legislature, while the Herald warned that sharing an officer with Interhall Council could mean trouble for both groups. An editorial the following week argued the Kentucky Intercollegiate State Legislature was worth keeping as a way to promote ideas.

events.title: Crosswalk resolution passes
events.body: The congress passed a resolution calling for a crosswalk. Campus safety items, including new screens for dormitory windows, filled much of the fall agenda.

events.title: Getting tough on absenteeism
events.body: ASG moved to get tough on absenteeism after a member lost his seat the week before. The Herald was simultaneously reporting that apathy was killing both ASG and the Residence Hall Association.

events.title: Constitutional amendments up for a vote
events.body: Constitutional amendments went before the body in November, in the same season the congress was pushing for required teacher evaluations. It was the third straight year of structural revision attempts.

events.title: ASG explains its empty seats
events.body: The organization publicly cited its reasons for the vacancies in its ranks, and four congress positions had been filled at a single meeting earlier that month. Days later an editorial told the body it needed better ideas, not gimmicks.

events.title: Ragland and Whitehouse win the primaries
events.body: Shannon Ragland and Scott Whitehouse won the ASG presidential primaries, narrowing a field of seven. The same issue reported passage of a proposal requesting a memorial area on campus.

events.title: Whitehouse elected; condom machines approved
events.body: Scott Whitehouse won the ASG presidential election, in an issue that also reported the congress approving condom machines for campus. The election coverage ran alongside editorials saying oversight and closed minds had marred the process.

events.title: Bruce Cambron calls for a new election
events.body: Bruce Cambron called for a new election a week after the results, following coverage of votes cast for a write-in candidate that ASG was told it could not ignore. The dispute carried into the following fall.

leaders.name: Scott Whitehouse
leaders.note: ASG filed a formal reaction to the General Education Task Force proposal in 1988.
profile: Whitehouse won the March 1988 ASG presidential primary alongside Shannon Ragland, emerging from a field of seven candidates in a year when only two of 32 congress positions were contested.

He won the presidency on 7 April 1988, in an election the Herald's own editorial pages said had been marred by oversight and closed minds, and amid coverage of votes for a write-in candidate that the congress was told it could not ignore.

The disputed election shadowed his term into the fall: Bruce Cambron, who had demanded a new election in April, took his complaint to university president Thomas Meredith in October 1988, weeks after the congress banned future write-in campaigns. His year also produced ASG's formal written reaction to the General Education Task Force proposal.

events.title: A formal reaction to the General Education Task Force
events.body: ASG filed a written response to a proposed overhaul of general education requirements - one of the earliest surviving examples of student government intervening in curriculum rather than campus life.

events.title: Write-in campaigns banned
events.body: ASG approved a ban on future write-in campaigns, five months after write-in votes had thrown its own presidential election into dispute. An editorial the next issue said the block showed ASG was not listening.

events.title: Freshman election turnout called pretty good
events.body: Turnout in the ASG freshman election was reported as "pretty good." The same issue said the organization was working to make the importance of voting register with students.

events.title: Cambron takes his election complaint to the president
events.body: Bruce Cambron, who had called for a new election in April, talked to university president Thomas Meredith about the ASG election. The spring's disputed result was still alive six months on.

events.title: Half the open slots filled; shelters for shuttle stops
events.body: ASG filled half of its open congress seats and sought shelters and seats for campus shuttle stops. The following week the Herald editorialized that ASG's efforts directly helped and served students.

events.title: The weeklong Thanksgiving break is dropped
events.body: ASG dropped its push for a weeklong Thanksgiving break, three weeks after voting to seek one. In the same issue, members rated their own organization as average.

events.title: An extra study day recommended
events.body: ASG recommended adding an extra study day before exams. The proposal followed January efforts to find a way to print teacher evaluations.

events.title: More movie hours wanted
events.body: The congress asked for more movie hours on campus. It was one of the quality-of-life items that filled the spring agenda before election season.

events.title: Amos Gott edges Lynn Groemling
events.body: Amos Gott narrowly defeated Lynn Groemling in the ASG presidential race. The campaign season had drawn complaints from candidates about the brief primary and an editorial warning that name recognition should not decide the race.

leaders.name: Amos Gott
leaders.note: The best-documented pre-1992 presidency in the archive. Signed correspondence survives on extended library hours, the DUC flagpole, the stadium press box and a local pizza vendor dispute.
profile: Gott was a visible member before he was president, signing Herald letters on ASG's behalf, including a January 1989 piece promoting Campus Pride '89 and an earlier letter urging readers to understand the organization.
He won the presidency in April 1989, edging Lynn Groemling in a race that had drawn candidate complaints about the brief primary.

His presidency ran on correspondence: resolutions went out over his signature as memoranda to named administrators and answers came back. In spring 1990 he wrote to six administrators under Resolution 90-6-S seeking changes to the final exam schedule, part of a surviving file that also covers extended library hours, the Downing University Center flagpole, mace sales at the bookstore, AIDS education and larger diplomas.

events.title: Extended library hours
events.body: Correspondence between President Amos Gott, Howard Bailey, Sally Ann Strickler and Michael Binder. Resolutions went out as letters to named administrators and answers came back.

events.title: The Downing University Center flagpole
events.body: One item in a working inventory of the job that year: the flagpole, the stadium press box, a dispute involving a local pizza vendor and a proposed budget for the Board of Student Body Presidents.

events.title: Gott gets a jump on the semester
events.body: The Herald reported that Amos Gott had gotten a jump on the ASG semester, opening his presidency before classes settled in. A companion piece urged students to participate in the organization.

events.title: A budget tiny compared to other schools
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG's budget was tiny compared to student governments at other schools. Two days later the congress approved joining a new board but admitted it could not afford the membership.

events.title: Resolution 89-3-F asks for AIDS education
events.body: Under Resolution 89-3-F, ASG corresponded with administrators requesting education on AIDS, HIV and sexually transmitted diseases. The letters survive in the SGA records alongside the year's other resolution correspondence on mace sales, larger diplomas and a food services committee.

events.title: Student government goes to Glasgow
events.body: Student government went to the WKU Glasgow campus, and the congress agreed to look again at a Public Interest Research Group. Both stories ran in the same mid-October issue.

events.title: PIRG sunk over its fee system
events.body: ASG voted down the proposed Public Interest Research Group, saying its fee system was the culprit. The decision ended a semester of on-and-off consideration of the group.

events.title: Congress votes to expand
events.body: ASG voted to expand its congress, a week after reporting it might add representatives. A follow-up story said classes and student groups would get more voice in the organization.

events.title: Withdrawals save an invalid primary
events.body: Candidates withdrew from the ASG races, saving a primary that would otherwise have been invalid; only two candidates were running for president. The Herald had already reported that interest in the organization might be lower, illustrated by a cartoon of student government in an empty room.

leaders.name: Michael Colvin
leaders.note: Elected Associated Student Government president in results the Herald reported on 19 April 1990; the 1991 Talisman independently confirms him as Associated Student Government President for that year.

profile: Michael Colvin won the Associated Student Government presidential election in results the Herald reported on 19 April 1990 under the headline "Michael Colvin Aces Associated Student Government Election." The 1991 Talisman independently lists him as Associated Student Government President for 1990-91.
In office, the Herald reported ASG considering a four-day class week (7 February 1991) and covered concern inside the organization over a change affecting student insurance (15 January 1991).
The archive does not preserve further detail of how the term ended or what Colvin did afterward.

Colvin took office in August 1990, introduced by the Herald as a new leader who wanted to make ideas reality. He had been active in the organization at least since September 1989, when he signed a Herald piece soliciting help for ASG.

His spring 1991 agenda was the widest of the era: in a single February week ASG moved to cap tuition boosts, proposed overhauling the Detrex registration system, and planned lobbying to protect student financial aid.
Letters he signed under Resolution 91-7-S survive in the SGA records, pressing administrators Kemble Johnson and Debby Cherwak for improvements to Detrex Field.

Legislative records fill out the year beyond what the Herald's brief items captured. In fall 1990 the body introduced bills for a roundtable of student organization presidents (Bill #90-2-F) and for microwaves in the cafeterias (Bill #90-4-F). On 29 November 1990 it passed Resolution 90-10-F asking for a left-handed desk in every classroom, and killed Resolution 90-12-F, which had asked that absences tied to Iben Browning's widely publicized New Madrid Fault earthquake prediction be excused; no earthquake came. In the spring the Senate suspended and amended its own by-laws in a short cluster of bills, including Bill #91-6-S changing the procedure for overriding a presidential veto - a procedure tested weeks later when the emergency-kit resolution survived a veto on 14 March 1991. The spring term also produced a resolution asking the university to improve Detrex Field, the intramural field, and bills on joining the Hilltopper Athletic Foundation, recognizing presidential scholars in the Herald, and a book exchange board for Grise Hall.

profile: Falmlen won the Associated Student Government presidency in results the Herald reported on 11 April 1991 under the headline "Heather Falmlen Wins Amid Associated Student Government Election Protests." A Herald "Meet the Candidates" feature on 2 April had previewed four contenders for the race: Falmlen, Rob Evans, Van Hodge, and Dan Knowles. The same 11 April issue reported a rival group urging students to boycott the vote, an editorial calling the contest's "immature antics" a disappointment, and a published complaint that the Herald's own election coverage had been biased.

In office, her administration fought a running battle over the makeup of the Board of Regents. On 29 October 1991 the Associated Student Government passed Resolution 91-6-F asking that Joe Iracane not be re-elected chair of the board; the Herald covered the vote the same day under "Associated Student Government Opposes Joseph Iracane." The board went ahead and re-elected him a week later, the university's own "On Campus" newsletter reported on 6 November. On 30 January 1992 the Herald reported the Associated Student Government was separately planning a committee aimed at student access to the regent, in the same issue that carried an editorial cartoon, "Ventriloquist's Dummy," targeting Falmlen. On 4 February 1992 the body passed Resolution 92-7-S, declaring its support for the WKU football program in spite of budget cuts; the Board of Regents voted that May to keep the program.

That fall the body passed Resolution 91-2-F, asking for a change to Big Red Shuttle bus fares, and held its regular fall senate elections in October, including a separate freshman senator election on 15 October.

The signature action of her term was procedural: on 7 April 1992 the Associated Students voted to rename itself the Student Government Association, a change students ratified in a referendum a week later, effective that autumn. WKU's own "On Campus" newsletter had confirmed on 22 May 1991, at the start of her term, that Falmlen held both the presidency and the student regent seat - the same dual role held by the presidents before and after her in this period. The archive does not preserve further detail of her regency or of what she did after her term.

Other legislative business that fall included Resolution 91-7-F, backing the renewal of President Thomas Meredith's contract by the Board of Regents; a bill funding a "President for a Day" fundraiser (Bill #91-09-F); a bill funding renovation of the ASG chambers (Bill #91-03-F); and a bill proposing a new organizational slogan (Bill #91-11-F), introduced the same season the body renamed itself from the Associated Students to the Student Government Association.

profile: Joe Rains was elected Associated Student Government president on 14 April 1992, a contested race the Herald's election-day issue covered with dueling opinion pieces: an editorial headlined "Associated Student Government Needs Joe Rains" ran alongside a cartoon depicting him as Darth Vader, and the paper carried separate profile pieces on candidates Mark Miller, Mistianna Holcomb and Melony Jones. The same ballot carried the referendum that renamed Associated Students as the Student Government Association; Rains took office that autumn as the first president to serve under the new name.

In office, Rains argued that SGA should support a campus student escort service (Herald, 10 December 1992) and took part in a rally at the state capitol in Frankfort urging the legislature to stop cuts to higher-education funding, for which the WKU University Senate commended him in Resolution R92.11.
The archive does not preserve further detail of how the term ended.

Rains ran for the presidency in April 1992 against Mistianna Holcomb, in the same election week that students voted on a referendum to rename the Associated Student Government as the Student Government Association. The Herald covered both races in a single issue, so his campaign and the rename were decided together.

On election day the Herald's opinion pages carried a letter headlined "Associated Student Government Needs Joe Rains" alongside a Patrick Richardson editorial cartoon depicting Rains as Darth Vader, a sign of how visible the race had become on campus.

The SGA's own list of presidents, published on its website in 2001, records Joe Rains of Nashville, Tennessee as the organization's 26th president, serving 1992-93, and marks him as having also served as student regent.

The digitised record of his year does not name him directly in any indexed description, but it carries one distinctive trace: the minutes for December 1, 1992 record plans for a call-in radio show the association titled 'Just Ask Joe,' alongside Project Western and President for a Day. The same year's minutes show a congress preoccupied with state budget cuts, tuition increases, student health insurance and repeated plans for a rally in Frankfort.

events.title: Joe Rains elected SGA president as the ASG-to-SGA renaming took effect
events.body: Rains won a contested Associated Student Government presidential election covered by the Herald under the headline "Associated Student Government Needs Joe Rains," alongside a rival editorial cartoon depicting him as Darth Vader and profile pieces on candidates Mark Miller, Mistianna Holcomb and Melony Jones. The same ballot carried the referendum renaming Associated Students as the Student Government Association.

events.title: Rains pushed SGA to back a student escort service
events.body: SGA president Joe Rains argued the organization should support a campus student escort service, the Herald reported.

events.title: University Senate honored Rains for a Frankfort budget-cut rally
events.body: The WKU University Senate adopted Resolution R92.11, commending SGA president Joe Rains for taking part in a rally at the state capitol in Frankfort asking the legislature to stop cuts to higher-education funding. TopSCHOLAR records the resolution's history running from 11 December 1992 to its adoption on 29 January 1993.

events.title: Rains takes office with a rename to carry out
events.body: The Herald reported that incoming president Joe Rains would oversee the change from Associated Student Government to Student Government Association, which students had ratified by referendum the week before. The new name took effect that fall, making Rains the first president to serve under it.

events.title: The renamed SGA elects its representatives
events.body: In its first weeks under the new name, the Student Government Association held elections for its representatives. The Herald covered the vote at the start of the fall semester.

events.title: Support gathers for a rally
events.body: The Herald's index for this issue records the new SGA winning support for a campus rally that October, under the headline "Student Government Association Gets Support for Rally."

events.title: An invitation to get involved
events.body: An opinion piece by Paul Weathers urged students to get involved in the Student Government Association, part of the Herald's running commentary on the body during its first semester under the new name.

events.title: Donald Smith rolls to victory
events.body: The Herald called the spring election with the headline "Student Government Association Election: Donald Smith Rolls to Victory." Smith would succeed Rains for the 1993-94 term.

events.title: Fall opened with a new logo and discount cards
events.body: At its first meeting of the fall on August 25, 1992, the student government discussed a new logo, student discount cards, a voter registration drive and committee assignments. The group was still transitioning from the Associated Student Government name to SGA, and its minutes from this year appear under both titles.

events.title: Resolution asked WKU to spare academics from budget cuts
events.body: Resolution 92-7-F asked the university to exempt academic units from a round of proposed budget cuts. State funding pressure ran through the whole fall; the same weeks produced repeated plans for a student rally in Frankfort.

events.title: President Meredith addressed the student congress
events.body: WKU President Thomas Meredith came to the October 13 meeting to talk about computers, laundry facilities, cable television, lighting and Potter Hall. The same minutes record discussion of budget cuts, homecoming elections, a newsletter and joint forums with the Residence Hall Association.

events.title: Congress honored the Lady Toppers
events.body: Resolution 92-8-F honored the WKU women's basketball team for its runner-up finish in the NCAA tournament. It was one of a string of numbered resolutions the congress produced that fall on subjects from drop-add fees to parking.

events.title: Just Ask Joe radio program and Project Western
events.body: The December 1 minutes record plans for a Just Ask Joe call-in radio program, the Project Western campus cleanup, a President for a Day event, recycling bins and student health insurance. The meeting closed out a semester dominated by tuition and budget worries.

events.title: Meredith returned to pitch Potter Hall as a student service center
events.body: President Thomas Meredith addressed the February 2 meeting about campus laundry, cable television and turning Potter Hall into a student service center. Members also discussed tuition increases, resignations and general education requirements.

events.title: Spring closed with elections and Earth Day plans
events.body: The April 13 meeting took up the budget, spring elections, the annual banquet, a one-card ID system, smoking policy, Adopt-a-Spot and Earth Day. It was the last full meeting recorded in the digitised minutes for the year.

events.title: Herald previews the race and the rename referendum
events.body: The Herald previewed the Associated Student Government presidential race under "Mistianna Holcomb, Joe Rains Vying for Presidency," profiled candidate Susan Mitchell under "Susan Mitchell Has a Fresh Perspective," and reported that students would soon vote on a referendum to rename the Associated Student Government the Student Government Association. No source found confirms what office Mitchell sought or whether she won it.

events.title: Turnout worries and candidate profiles filled the ballot issue
events.body: The same issue that reported Rains' win ran the Herald's concern piece "Many Students Won't Vote" alongside profile pieces on the other candidates: "Mark Miller's Involvement Makes Him a Leader," "Mistianna Holcomb Takes a Stand for Students," and "Melony Jones Loved & Respected by Peers."

senate.note: Minutes from 25 Aug 1992 through 13 Apr 1993 survive, recording a congress occupied with state budget cuts, tuition increases and a Frankfort rally, but no full officer list, committee structure, or seat count survives beyond the president.

leaders.name: Donald Smith
leaders.note: Later president of the College Heights Foundation. Interviewed by the Herald in 2022 on what has and has not changed. At least seventeen numbered resolutions survive from autumn 1993 - the fullest single-semester record in the collection.

sources.label: Herald - The making of an SGA president

profile: Smith won the April 1993 election decisively. The Herald's headline was "Student Government Association Election: Donald Smith Rolls to Victory."

That September the Herald profiled the new president under the headline "Donald Smith Followed Grandfather's Lead All the Way to President's Office," tracing a family connection to the role he had just taken up.

Smith, from Elizabethtown, went on to become president of the College Heights Foundation. Interviewed by the Herald in 2022, he said that while the structure had changed over the years, "the fundamental principle for SGA to be a voice for the students has remained unphased," and that if SGA improves over time the WKU experience improves with it.

events.title: At least seventeen numbered resolutions in one semester
events.body: Resolutions 93-4-F through 93-20-F survive in the correspondence files - the fullest single-semester record in the collection, and the best available answer to how much a WKU student senate actually passes in a working term.

events.title: A delayed constitution reading
events.body: The fall semester opened with a stumble. The Herald reported that a scheduled reading of the SGA constitution had been delayed, in the same issue that covered rising tempers over campus parking.

events.title: Congress changes approved
events.body: The SGA approved changes to its congress in September while freshmen debated for open positions. The Herald covered both in a single mid-September issue.

events.title: Let's work together for change
events.body: The Herald ran an opinion piece under the heading "Let's Work Together for Change" and put the question of how SGA could reach more students to its People Poll. The paper also ran a Stacy Curtis editorial cartoon offering a "recipe for better representation."

events.title: A resolution on class attendance
events.body: An SGA resolution covered by the Herald would have let students skip class, reported under the headline "Attendance: Student Government Association Resolution Would Let Students Skip Class."

events.title: A disputed primary
events.body: The Herald reported that presidential candidate Scott Sivley had not followed SGA and university procedures during the election, in the same issue that carried the tallied results of the primary. The episode ran alongside the paper's get-out-the-vote editorial coverage.

events.title: Evans and Higdon ready to lead
events.body: The Herald closed the election season with "Rob Evans & Tara Higdon Ready to Lead Students." The same issue carried letters both defending the organization and, from future president Kristen Miller, a piece headlined "Student Government Association Defends Itself."

events.title: A new constitution came up first
events.body: Bill 93-1-F, introduced at the second meeting of the fall, proposed amendments to the SGA constitution. Constitutional revision stayed on the agenda through October, alongside the tuition rally the congress was planning.

events.title: Congress planned a tuition rally
events.body: The October 12 meeting discussed a tuition rally, the budget, the Plus System and parking. The rally kept appearing in the minutes for the next month as tuition increases moved through the state process.

events.title: Bill funded emergency phones on campus
events.body: Bill 93-6-F proposed purchasing and installing emergency telephones on campus. The Herald was still reporting on SGA's security phones the following February, and campus lighting and safety stayed on the agenda into the spring.

events.title: Memorial trees for students who die while enrolled
events.body: Bill 93-12-F proposed planting memorial trees in tribute to students who die while enrolled at WKU. It capped a heavy late-November run of legislation that also included child care grants for non-traditional students, a book exchange and opening the Downing University Center computer lab during finals.

events.title: President for a Day swapped a student into Meredith's office
events.body: The Herald reported that student Angelo Rodriguez would switch places with President Thomas Meredith through SGA's President for a Day program. The same issue covered SGA's security phones on campus and a proposal to let students retake C grades that was killed in committee.

events.title: A $3 fee to support the Big Red Card
events.body: Resolution 94-4-S proposed a three dollar student fee to support the Big Red Card program. The card system and its fees ran through the minutes for the rest of the spring.

events.title: Willard's resignation reached the floor
events.body: The March 29 meeting took up the resignation of basketball coach Ralph Willard along with the Big Red Card fee, teacher evaluations, emergency telephones, campus lighting and the coming elections. Dialogue Day and Adopt-a-Spot rounded out a crowded agenda.

events.title: A year-end banquet, and corners cut on the budget
events.body: The Herald closed the year with two SGA stories: the year-end banquet recognizing award winners and officers, and a report that the association was cutting corners with its budget.

leaders.name: Robert Evans

sources.label: WKU Board of Regents, quarterly meeting, 22 Sep 1995
WKU Board of Regents, quarterly meeting, 15 Aug 1994

profile: Running for president in April 1994, Evans was profiled by the Herald as the candidate who urged discussion of the issues. He faced Scott Sivley in a contested race; on election day, 19 April, the Herald reported Sivley had been warned by SGA for violating the organization's campaign policies, alongside an opinion piece urging a vote for "Rob Evans, Tara Higdon" and another arguing that "Sacrificing Student Government Association Means Saving Needed Programs." The same issue's editorial pages told students "The Choice Is Yours" in the SGA vote.
He won, and the Herald introduced the incoming leadership with "Rob Evans & Tara Higdon Ready to Lead Students." Higdon, elected alongside him, would succeed him as president a year later.

The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Robert Evans of Owensboro as the 28th president, serving 1994-95, and marks him as having also served as student regent. The Board of Regents' quarterly meeting of 15 August 1994 swore him in alongside Joy Gramling and Cornelius Martin, and carried resolutions of appreciation for outgoing officers Donald Smith - his predecessor as SGA president and student regent - and Monnie Hankins. The Board's quarterly meeting of 22 September 1995 - the start of the following academic year - swore in Tara Higdon as his successor on the board, marking the end of his regency.

After his year leading the WKU student body, Rob Evans kept a statewide role: in April 1996 the Herald profiled him under the headline 'Rob Evans Representing Students from Across State,' describing his seat on the Kentucky Council on Higher Education, the body that then oversaw the state's public universities.

events.title: The 1994-95 budget passes
events.body: The SGA approved its budget for the year in early September, reported by the Herald under "Student Government Association Approves Budget for 1994-95."

events.title: Campus security shapes the spring campaign
events.body: The Herald reported that being stalked had influenced candidate Tara Higdon, putting campus security at the center of the spring election coverage.

events.title: Visibility key to SGA success
events.body: As the year closed, the Herald's opinion pages argued that visibility was the key to the organization's success, illustrated with a Stacy Curtis editorial cartoon of student government in a glass box.

events.title: A new beginning
events.body: The Herald's transition piece, "Tara Higdon Sees New Beginning," marked the handover from Robert Evans to his elected successor at the end of the academic year.

events.title: Expanded shuttle service draws attention
events.body: The Herald reported that expanded Big Red Shuttle bus service, a route the Student Government Association had pushed to extend, was drawing enthusiasm from local stores along its new stops.

events.title: An editorial defends the memorial trees
events.body: The same issue carried the opinion piece "Don't Destroy Trees," addressing the fate of the memorial trees the SGA had established the previous year to honor students who died while enrolled.

events.title: Evans defeats Sivley for the SGA presidency
events.body: Rob Evans faced Scott Sivley at the polls on election day; the Herald reported the same day that Sivley had been warned by SGA for violating the organization's campaign policies. Evans and running mate Tara Higdon won.

src.label: Herald 69:52 [51], 19 Apr 1994, "Student Government Association Elections: Scott Sivley vs. Rob Evans at Polls Today"

events.title: Campus assesses storm damage
events.body: The Herald reported that WKU's campus suffered less damage than the surrounding city after a tornado, the same week as the SGA election.

src.label: Herald 69:52 [51], 19 Apr 1994, "Storm; Campus Suffered Less Damage than City"

events.title: Resolution asks for grades before the "W" deadline
events.body: SGA passed Resolution 94-11-F, asking that students be given a grade before the end of the withdrawal ("W") period so they could make an informed decision about dropping a class.

src.label: SGA Resolution 94-11-F, Examination Prior to end of "W" Period

events.title: Bill seeks an SGA listing in the phone book
events.body: SGA introduced Bill 94-8-F, asking that a Student Government Association directory section be added to the university's telephone book.

events.title: Evans sworn in as student regent
events.body: The Board of Regents' quarterly meeting swore in Robert Evans, Joy Gramling and Cornelius Martin, and carried resolutions of appreciation for outgoing officers Donald Smith - the previous SGA president and student regent - and Monnie Hankins.

src.label: WKU Board of Regents, quarterly meeting, 15 Aug 1994

events.title: Security phone tops SGA's spring to-do list
events.body: The Herald reported a new security phone, a shuttle stop, and the memorial trees on the Student Government Association's agenda, under "New Security Phone, Shuttle Stop, Trees Lead to Student Government's To Do List." The same issue reported a mystery caller had been scaring students with stalking and harassment, the incident that would shape the spring campaign two months later.

src.label: Herald 70:32, 24 Jan 1995, "New Security Phone, Shuttle Stop, Trees Lead to Student Government's To Do List"

events.title: SGA discusses escort service, campus cleanup
events.body: SGA's regular meeting took up the student escort service, a "President for a Day" promotion, a campus cleanup, and open positions on the body.

events.title: Tara Higdon moved up as turnout moved down
events.body: The Herald reported the spring election under the headline 'Tara Higdon Moves Up; Voting Down,' recording both the choice of the next president and a drop in voter participation. The election closed out the 1994-95 administration.

events.title: The Herald called visibility the key to SGA's success
events.body: As the year ended, the Herald ran an editorial package on the association, pairing a Stacy Curtis cartoon of student government in a glass box with the editorial 'Visibility Key to Student Government Association Success.' It was a summing-up of a year in which the paper pressed SGA to be seen doing its work.

src.label: Herald 69:52, 21 Apr 1994, "Rob Evans & Tara Higdon Ready to Lead Students"

executive.name: Tara Higdon
executive.note: A Slaughters junior; succeeded Evans as president and as student regent the following year.

src.label: Herald 69:52, 21 Apr 1994, "Rob Evans & Tara Higdon Ready to Lead Students"

leaders.name: Tara (Higdon) Howard
leaders.note: Plaque gives maiden name in parentheses - confirmed under Higdon. Named as SGA president for 1995-96 in Herald election coverage ("Tara Higdon Moves Up; Voting Down," 11 Apr 1995) and again as outgoing president in the 1996 succession coverage; the 1994-95 organization record independently names her as that year's Administrative Vice President, noting she would succeed Evans as president and student regent the following year.
profile: Higdon's path to the presidency ran through the campus security debates of 1995. During the spring campaign the Herald reported that her experience of being stalked had influenced her, under the headline "Campus Security: Stalking Influenced Tara Higdon."

After a year as part of the elected leadership alongside Robert Evans, she won the presidency, and the Herald marked the transition with "Tara Higdon Sees New Beginning." Her term brought new emergency phones, a skywalk proposal, a campus store proposal and a push for longer visitation hours.
The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Tara D. Higdon of Slaughters as the 29th president, serving 1995-96, and marks her as having also served as student regent.

Higdon won the presidency in April 1995, with the Herald reporting the result under the headline 'Tara Higdon Moves Up; Voting Down' - she moved up to the top office even as voter turnout fell. The paper's year-end editorial the following week argued that visibility would be the key to the association's success.

Her year ended in a contested, four-way race to succeed her, and Higdon took a public side: her letter 'Vote for Kristin Miller' ran in the Herald's April 16, 1996 issue, in the same election-week pages as the candidates' debate coverage and the campaign for SGA's constitutional amendments.

The spring of her term was the stormiest stretch in the association's decade of Herald coverage: within a single week in February 1996 the paper carried both SGA's skywalk proposal for the bottom of the Hill and a letter dismissing the association as a 'puppet' group, and by late April a columnist was asking whether students cared about student government at all.

events.title: Two more emergency phones
events.body: The year opened with a security win. The Herald reported that SGA had put two more emergency phones on campus, continuing the safety agenda that had shaped the previous spring's election.

events.title: A dress code, and a call for interest
events.body: September coverage included an SGA dress code and a piece headlined "Tara Higdon Seeks Student Interest in Group," as the new president worked to draw students into the organization.

events.title: Presidential pay compared
events.body: The Herald reported that pay for student government presidents was higher at other schools, an early airing of a compensation question that would recur in later decades.

events.title: A skywalk at the bottom of the Hill
events.body: SGA proposed a skywalk at the bottom of the Hill, and the Herald also reported the organization bringing emergency phones to campus in the same issue. The skywalk would quickly draw editorial fire.

events.title: The Herald pushes back
events.body: Five days after the skywalk proposal, the Herald told SGA to "ditch the pie-in-the-sky idea," and its letters page carried Richard Malek's charge that the organization acted as a "puppet" group. Another letter defended officers Horace Johnson and Kristen Miller against the label "hair-brained."

events.title: A new store on campus
events.body: SGA proposed a new store on campus, reported by the Herald in early March as the organization kept generating campus improvement ideas through the spring.

events.title: Longer visitation hours
events.body: SGA asked the university for longer residence hall visitation hours, one of the quality-of-life requests that defined the organization's agenda that spring.

events.title: A student credited SGA for its trees
events.body: A Herald opinion piece ran under the headline 'Student Government Association Doing Good Job with Trees,' crediting the association's campus planting work. Trees and campus grounds were among the group's most visible projects that year.

events.title: SGA proposed a skywalk at the bottom of the Hill
events.body: The Herald reported SGA's proposal for a pedestrian skywalk at the bottom of the Hill, and the same issue covered its push to bring emergency phones to campus. The skywalk became the most argued-about SGA idea of the spring.

events.title: The skywalk drew fire within a week
events.body: Five days after the proposal, the Herald ran a column telling SGA to 'ditch' the 'pie-in-the-sky' skywalk idea, and a letter in the same issue called the association a 'puppet' group. The episode set the combative tone of the spring semester.

events.title: A campus store proposal followed
events.body: SGA proposed a new store on campus, the Herald reported, as the association kept generating campus improvement ideas through the spring. A week earlier the paper had covered its wish to see the next university president promoted from within.

events.title: Four candidates ran for the top office
events.body: The Herald reported that four students were running for SGA president. The campaign filled the opinion pages for the next three weeks, with endorsements, a debate and a proposed slate of constitutional amendments on the ballot.

events.title: A test-free week before finals
events.body: SGA proposed a test-free week before finals, one of the last legislative pushes of the year. The idea ran in the Herald alongside Board of Regents coverage of fee increases.

events.title: Debate, amendments and endorsements filled election week
events.body: The Herald covered the presidential debate under the headline 'Debate Reflects Attitudes,' while letters urged a yes vote on SGA's constitutional amendments. Outgoing officer Tara Higdon's letter backing Kristen Miller ran on the same pages.

events.title: New officers sworn in as a columnist shrugged
events.body: The Herald reported the swearing-in of SGA's new officers for 1996-97. A column in the same issue, 'Students Just Don't Care About Student Government Association,' summed up the year's running argument about relevance.

executive.note: A Slaughters junior; had served as Administrative Vice President and student regent in 1994-95 before moving up to the presidency.

leaders.name: Kristen Miller
leaders.note: Confirmed by Herald 71:54 (18 Apr 1996, election coverage headlined "It's Kristen Miller's Time") and Herald 72:46 (27 Mar 1997, term-end reflection piece), both naming her SGA president in the plaque year.

sources.label: Herald, 2 Feb 2016 - Ransdell retirement means search for new president

profile: Miller had been a Herald columnist and an SGA officer before winning the presidency; her letters in the paper defending the organization date to 1994. In her first weeks as president in August 1996 she made a plan to drive party-goers home, the beginning of what became the Provide-A-Ride service.

As student body president she was the student representative on the committee searching for WKU's ninth president. Interviewed in 2016, she recalled serious talk of cutting football or academic programs, saying "there was one pot of money everyone was fighting over," and described how a late-arriving alumnus candidate named Gary Ransdell impressed the committee by pulling out a binder full of plans after his interview.

In March 1997 the Herald ran "Kristen Miller Reflects on Year as Student Government Association President" as her term wound down. The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Kristen L. Miller of Louisville as the 30th president and marks her as having also served as student regent.

Miller won the SGA presidency in April 1996 at the end of a four-way race, with the Herald's news coverage declaring 'It's Kristen Miller's Time.' A week earlier the paper had profiled her campaign under the headline 'Kristen Miller Focuses on Experience in Student Government Association.'

Days into the fall semester, the Herald reported 'Kristen Miller Makes Plan to Drive Party-Goers Home.' The idea became Provide-a-Ride, the safe-ride program that appears in SGA's minutes throughout 1996-97 and was still being funded by the congress years later.

Near the end of her term, the Herald ran 'Kristen Miller Reflects on Year as Student Government Association President,' looking back on a year that included the creation of a Technology Committee, the Provide-a-Ride launch and SGA's narrow vote to back adding sexual orientation to Western's anti-discrimination policy.

events.title: A retreat opens the year
events.body: The Herald reported that an SGA retreat provided the opportunity for new discussion and legislation, setting the agenda for Kristen Miller's term before classes had fully begun.

events.title: A plan to drive party-goers home
events.body: The Herald reported "Kristen Miller Makes Plan to Drive Party-Goers Home," the earliest indexed coverage of the safe-ride idea that became Provide-A-Ride. The same issue reported SGA giving more money to campus clubs.

events.title: Thirty years of student government
events.body: The Herald's Homecoming edition carried Kim Leonard's feature "Student Government Association Has Grown in 30 Years," marking three decades since the Associated Students' founding in 1966.

events.title: Extending the shuttle route
events.body: SGA pushed to have the campus shuttle route extended, reported by the Herald in mid-November.

events.title: Provide-A-Ride needs support
events.body: The Herald reported that Provide-A-Ride needed SGA and student support to survive its first year. The service would outlast the doubts and still be running as a free weekend van service years later.

events.title: A seat at the presidential search
events.body: Resolution 97-4-S addressed the Presidential Search Committee as WKU sought a successor to Thomas Meredith, and Bill 97-3-S contributed to the WKU Senior Class Campaign the same day. The search ended with the hiring of Gary Ransdell later that year.

events.title: Reaching beyond campus
events.body: In one April session the body passed Resolution 97-13-S to reactivate the Kentucky Students Association and Resolution 97-14-S to establish a student representative position on the Council for Postsecondary Education, pushing WKU student interests into state-level policy.

events.title: Candidates prepare, and fire alarms get a deadline
events.body: The Herald covered candidates preparing for the spring elections alongside an SGA effort seeking faster shut-off times for fire alarms, a snapshot of the organization's mix of politics and practical fixes.

events.title: Officers sworn in at the first fall meeting
events.body: The August 27 meeting swore in officers and took up the retreat, an open house, the budget and homecoming. It opened the first full year of minutes in the digitised record since 1994.

events.title: SGA created a Technology Committee
events.body: The September 17 meeting created the SGA Technology Committee and discussed intramural facilities, photocopiers in dorms and Campus Clean Up. Student email accounts and other technology questions recur in the fall's minutes.

events.title: More lights proposed, and a veto recorded
events.body: The Herald reported SGA proposing more campus lighting while a resolution was vetoed. Campus lighting had been a steady SGA cause since the earlier emergency phones push.

events.title: SGA followed the presidential search
events.body: With Thomas Meredith's departure looming, the March 25 meeting discussed the university's presidential search along with an Orientation, Admissions and Registration Pal program, the Bridging the Gap forum and Campus Clean Up.

events.title: An anti-discrimination stand passed by a slim margin
events.body: The Herald reported that SGA passed a measure calling for gays to be included in Western's anti-discrimination policy by a slim margin, a week after covering the proposal's introduction. A letter in the same issue congratulated both SGA and the paper.

events.title: The year closed with a memorial tree dedication
events.body: The last recorded meeting of the year discussed the memorial tree dedication, elections, Earth Day, Thomas Meredith, Campus Clean Up, off-campus housing scholarships and a residence hall privatization study.

events.title: Few turn out for the election that chose Miller
events.body: The same Herald issue that declared "It's Kristen Miller's Time" also ran the headline "Few Turn Out for Election," continuing the decade's pattern of falling voter participation in SGA races.

events.title: Roller blades, skateboards, and a technology push
events.body: A September 24 meeting took up campus rules on roller blading and skateboards alongside Provide-A-Ride, a voter registration drive, a bonfire, Big Red Roar, the budget, and student email accounts.

events.title: Website, vacancies, and bylaws open the spring
events.body: The January 21 meeting discussed the organization's website, Provide-A-Ride, open vacancies on the body, the budget, and the by-laws, as the congress organized itself for the spring semester.

committees.name: Technology Committee
committees.note: Created at the 17 September 1996 meeting to take up student email accounts and other technology questions.

senate.note: Archive does not preserve a full senate officer list or seat count for this year.

leaders.name: Keith Coffman
