leaders.note: Outgoing letters from this period cover the Dogwood Drive crosswalk and student seating at athletic events. Confirmed by Herald 72:54 (24 Apr 1997, "Keith Coffman Takes Charge") and the SGA's own 2001 presidents list naming him the 31st president, 1997-98.
profile: Coffman presided over one of the busiest legislative years in the surviving 1990s record. The SGA's own legislation archive for 1997 preserves at least 24 numbered bills and resolutions from his fall semester alone, from the Dogwood Drive crosswalk to the ten-point grade scale, student e-mail addresses in the directory and ice machines in every residence hall.

The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Keith Coffman of Russellville as the 31st president, serving 1997-98, and marks him as having also served as student regent. His term coincided with Gary Ransdell's first year as university president.

Coffman's presidency opened with the Herald's April 24, 1997 headline 'Keith Coffman Takes Charge,' paired with a story in the same issue in which the new Student Government Association president mapped out his upcoming term.

events.title: A crosswalk on Dogwood Drive
events.body: One of a run of outgoing letters in these years covering student seating at athletic events, ice machines in residence halls, campus safety, professors posting office hours, food court hours, housing scholarships for off-campus students and student health services.

events.title: More student seats at the games
events.body: SGA secretary Jamie Fite wrote to interim president Barbara Burch requesting additional student seating in Diddle Arena and Smith Stadium. The letter survives in the SGA records collection.

events.title: The ten-point scale fight begins
events.body: Resolution 97-6-F called for reinstatement of the ten-point grade scale, and Resolution 97-5-F addressed charitable organizations and solicitation of funds the same evening. The grading fight would run on for years at WKU.

events.title: A career fair for summer jobs
events.body: Bill 97-1-F funded a Summer Job and Internship Career Fair, the first bill of the fall session under Keith Coffman.

events.title: Designated driver cards
events.body: Bill 97-3-F funded designated driver cards, extending the safe-ride agenda begun under Kristen Miller into a second year. The same week brought a bill to buy typewriters for the library.

events.title: A November flood of resolutions
events.body: Between November 2 and 18 the congress passed at least fifteen numbered resolutions, covering a speed hump for the Regents Avenue lot, fifteen-minute parking spaces, working ID scanners, new sidewalks at Thompson and Grise, ice machines, soap and sanitary restrooms in residence halls, picnic tables, bicycle racks and recognition for honors graduates. It is one of the densest legislative months in the surviving 1990s record.

events.title: Housing stipends for off-campus students
events.body: Jamie Fite wrote to Academic Affairs Vice President Barbara Burch about applying housing stipends to off-campus housing, following up resolutions on the subject passed in both 1997 sessions.

events.title: Spring bills: watch signs and a teaching award
events.body: The spring session's surviving record includes Bill 98-4-S for Neighborhood Watch signs on April 19 and Bill 98-5-S creating an Excellence in Teaching Award on April 21.

events.title: A push for action on stalled legislation
events.body: As the term closed, secretary Jamie Fite wrote to Provost Barbara Burch requesting action on several pieces of legislation, pressing the administration to answer what the congress had passed.

events.title: Keith Coffman took charge
events.body: The Herald announced the new administration with 'Keith Coffman Takes Charge,' and a companion piece reported the new president mapping his upcoming term. His term began as the spring semester closed.

events.title: Paper towels for the Downing University Center
events.body: Resolution 97-9-F asked that paper towels be placed in the restrooms of the Downing University Center. It is one of only two pieces of legislation from the year in the digitised SGA collection.

events.title: Picnic tables for the bottom of campus
events.body: Resolution 97-23-F requested picnic tables for the campus area near Zacharias Hall, Meredith Hall and Pearce-Ford Tower. Its numbering shows the congress had produced at least 23 fall resolutions by mid-November.

events.title: Coffman gets high marks as candidates line up
events.body: The Herald ran "Keith Coffman Served Students Well" alongside a People Poll asking students what they thought of his job performance, in the same issue that reported candidates preparing for the spring election.

events.title: A $15,000 electronic sign and a campaign for scholarships
events.body: In election week the Herald polled students on how they would spend $15,000 of SGA's money, ran a column arguing the money for a big electronic message sign could be better used, and printed dueling letters on whether the association served students. Its campaign coverage reported that candidate Stephanie Cosby wanted more scholarships.

events.title: Stephanie Cosby rolled to a huge victory
events.body: The Herald reported 'Stephanie Cosby Rolls to Huge Victory' in the SGA election that closed the year, alongside a story on how taxing election day was for officer candidates. Cosby would lead the association in 1998-99.

executive.name: Jamie Fite
executive.note: Signed outgoing SGA correspondence to the administration throughout the year, on athletic seating, housing stipends and stalled legislation.

senate.note: The archive preserves at least 24 numbered bills and resolutions from the fall 1997 session alone and a further spring 1998 session, but no full officer list or seat count survives beyond the president and secretary.

leaders.name: Stephanie Cosby
leaders.note: Letters survive on ice machines in the residence halls, campus safety, food court hours and professors posting office hours. Confirmed as SGA president for 1998-99 by Herald election coverage ("Stephanie Cosby Rolls to Huge Victory," 30 Apr 1998) and by the Kentucky Board of Student Body Presidents' fall 1998 dues letter addressed to her by name and title.
profile: Cosby is documented in office from the start of the 1998 fall semester, when the Kentucky Board of Student Body Presidents billed its dues in a memo addressed to "SGA president Stephanie Cosby." Her congress passed at least thirteen numbered bills that fall, from Murray State fire relief to Bookswap.com, and her officers answered public charges of unproductiveness with a written record of what had passed.
The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Stephanie Cosby of Greenville as the 32nd president, serving 1998-99, and marks her as having also served as student regent.

Cosby campaigned on financial aid, with the Herald's election-week coverage reporting that she wanted more scholarships. She won the presidency in a rout: the paper's April 30, 1998 election story ran under the headline 'Stephanie Cosby Rolls to Huge Victory,' next to a report on how taxing election day had been for the officer candidates.

Midway through her term she picked up a second title, with the Herald reporting 'Stephanie Cosby Named Queen of Hill' at homecoming in October 1998. Her year in office produced a steady advising-reform push, the failed University Boulevard widening request, the Kappa Alpha aid fight, and ended with the Judicial Council overturning the election to choose her successor.

events.title: Dues to the state association
events.body: The treasurer of the Kentucky Board of Student Body Presidents wrote to president Stephanie Cosby requesting payment of the 1998-99 dues, evidence of WKU's continuing seat at the state student leadership table.

events.title: Relief funds for Murray State
events.body: Bill 98-2-F allocated funds to the Murray State University Fire Relief Fund after the fatal Hester Hall dormitory fire that September, one of the rare occasions the body directed money off campus.

events.title: A coffee house for Pride Week and a Homecoming float
events.body: In a single October session the congress passed Bill 98-5-F funding a coffee house for Pride Week and Bill 98-6-F funding a joint SGA and Hillraiser Homecoming float. The fall slate also included a W.O.W. conference, ashtrays outside residence halls and an SGA survey.

events.title: An anonymous complaint about the room
events.body: An anonymous congress member wrote to the Executive Council about the tone and mood of SGA meetings. Mitchell Bailey issued a written response a week later, and both documents survive in the SGA records collection.

events.title: Betting on Bookswap.com
events.body: Bill 98-12-F had SGA sponsor Bookswap.com, an early attempt to use the web against textbook prices, and Bill 98-13-F funded the 1999 Camp Fair the next day to close the fall session.

events.title: Answering the charge of doing nothing
events.body: Vice president Matthew Bastin circulated a memo of the fall's passed legislation to the SGA advisor, officers, committee heads and the Herald's editor, answering accusations that SGA had been unproductive. The list itself was the rebuttal.

events.title: Concerns about student health services
events.body: Vice president Matthew Bastin wrote to president Gary Ransdell expressing SGA's concerns about student health services, closing the year by taking a student welfare issue to the top of the administration.

events.title: Dorm sprinklers and an advisor checklist
events.body: The Herald reported SGA wanted sprinklers added in the dorms, while Bill 98-1-F created a checklist of questions for students to ask their advisors. Days earlier the paper had counted the association's legislative efforts trailing the previous year, and a letter in this issue accused it of wasting time and money.

events.title: SGA asked for a wider University Boulevard
events.body: Resolution 98-7-F requested that University Boulevard be widened and that a traffic island be added for pedestrians. The Herald reported the following week that the University Boulevard proposal had failed, but the advising checklist was approved and grew into a run of advising-reform legislation through the fall.

events.title: The SGA president was crowned homecoming queen
events.body: The Herald reported 'Stephanie Cosby Named Queen of Hill' at homecoming. SGA had its own stake in the festivities that fall, funding a joint homecoming float with the Hillraisers.

events.title: A bill to help the burned-out Kappa Alphas
events.body: Bill 98-10-F proposed allocating funds to the Kappa Alpha fraternity after its house burned. The proposal set off the sharpest fight of the fall.

events.title: The Kappa Alpha aid vote failed, loudly
events.body: The Herald reported some SGA members were upset after the group voted down aid to the fraternity, and a companion letter said SGA had 'abandoned' the Kappa Alphas. Letters defending and attacking the decision ran for the rest of the semester.

events.title: Turbulent elections declared complete
events.body: The Herald reported the spring elections finished under the headline 'Turbulent Elections Complete,' while an opinion piece charged that SGA offered no leadership and a letter questioned the probe of candidate Will Jones. The turbulence was not over.

events.title: The Judicial Council overturned the election
events.body: The Herald reported that SGA's Judicial Council overturned the spring election, with coverage centering on candidate Joe Matheis, an editorial cartoon on nasty campaigns, and an opinion piece describing a 'swath of scandal' around the elections.

events.title: A final rush of legislation amid the election mess
events.body: Two days later the Herald reported SGA passing a final rush of legislation, while the election fallout continued in the letters column and a story urged students to vote again on Monday. The same issue introduced the incoming president as a self-described workaholic.

executive.name: Stephanie Cosby
executive.note: Of Greenville; also served as student regent.

src.label: Herald 73:53, 30 Apr 1998, "Stephanie Cosby Rolls to Huge Victory"

executive.name: Matthew Bastin
executive.note: Circulated the fall 1998 legislative record to answer charges of unproductiveness, and wrote to president Gary Ransdell on student health services in April 1999.

executive.office: Officer (title not specified in the archive)
executive.name: Mitchell Bailey
executive.note: Issued the Executive Council's written response to an anonymous congress member's complaint about the tone of SGA meetings, November 1998.

senate.note: Congress numbered its fall 1998 legislation sequentially, at least 98-1-F through 98-13-F, covering everything from an advisor checklist to Murray State fire relief; no full senate officer list, committee structure, or seat count survives beyond the executive officers named in the record.

documents.title: Resolution 98-7-F, University Boulevard widening, 6 Oct 1998
documents.summary: SGA's resolution asking WKU to widen University Boulevard and add a pedestrian traffic island. The Herald reported the following week that the request had failed even as a companion advising-checklist bill was approved and grew into a run of advising-reform legislation that fall.
documents.extract: Requested the widening of University Boulevard and a pedestrian traffic island.

documents.title: Bill 98-10-F, aid to Kappa Alpha after fire, 17 Nov 1998
documents.summary: SGA's bill proposing funds for the Kappa Alpha fraternity after its house burned. It set off the sharpest fight of the fall: the Herald reported the following month that the congress voted the aid down, and letters defending and attacking the decision ran for the rest of the semester.
documents.extract: Proposed allocating SGA funds to Kappa Alpha after its house fire.

leaders.name: Amanda Lich
leaders.note: Every contemporaneous 1999-2000 source found - the Herald's election and reflection coverage, the SGA's own website, and the organization's 2001 list of former presidents - gives her name as Amanda J. Coates or Amanda Coates, never Lich. A WKU employee working today in the university's Philanthropy & Alumni Engagement office in Bowling Green goes by Amanda Coates Lich; the combined surname is consistent with Coates being a maiden name and Lich a married name, but no source found ties that person directly to the 1999-2000 SGA presidency. The plaque's "Lich" is flagged here, not confirmed.

sources.label: WKU SGA site, home page (archived Aug 2000)
Herald 75:55, 25 Apr 2000, "Amanda Coates Reflects on Year as President"

profile: Contemporaneous records give her name as Amanda J. Coates. The SGA's own 2001 list of presidents records Amanda J. Coates of Brownsville as the 33rd president, serving 1999-2000, and marks her as having also served as student regent. The organization's website during and just after her term consistently refers to "President Amanda Coates."

She won the presidency in a contested April 1999 race against Will Jones, in results so close the Coates-Martin ticket demanded a recount: the initial 616-611 tally over Jones and running mate Kara Yeckering narrowed to 614-611 on the recount. A write-in ticket, Dwight Campbell and Kerri Richardson, took 145 votes. The same election saw a bitter down-ballot fight for vice president of finance, where Joe Matheis beat Ryan Morrison 700-688 only after SGA's judicial council reviewed - and let stand - his victory over a campaign-flier violation, and a Herald letter to the editor questioned SGA's handling of an investigation into racially charged fliers that had targeted Jones, the first Black SGA presidential candidate in years. The Herald's pre-election issue had separately reported SGA questioning an election-eve pizza party Jones held, and a debate over dropping the rule requiring a year of SGA service before running for office.

Her signature project was publishing faculty evaluations. From February 2000 she led meetings with the university president, the Faculty Senate chair and the senate's executive committee, and in April she co-authored Resolution 00-2-S with Adam Howard asking the Faculty Senate to approve a mandatory published evaluation beginning that fall.

At the end of her term the SGA website opened with the words "What SGA has done for you," showcasing three things: the faculty evaluations project, the fight over the Vice President of Student Affairs position and the Provide-A-Ride service. It is as close to a self-written record of her administration's priorities as survives.

As her term closed, the Herald ran an exit interview, "Amanda Coates Reflects on Year as President," in its April 25, 2000 issue. The election to succeed her, held in late March 2000, was contested between Cassie Martin and Duan Wright; Martin won, and by the following issue the Herald was asking the incoming president to "stand up on tough issues" while confirming that the faculty evaluations Coates had championed would be conducted and published starting that fall.

The Herald introduced the incoming 1999-2000 president on April 22, 1999 under the headline 'New Student Government Association Leader Workaholic.' The paper's index records the new leader's name as Amanda Coates, and she took office in the aftermath of a spring election that SGA's Judicial Council had overturned two days earlier.

Her congress spent the fall of 1999 building institutions: it created an Information Technology Director and website guidelines, established a senior awards banquet and hall of distinguished seniors, launched the toll-free Topline activity line, and publicly opposed an administrative move in Student Affairs while asking that Vice President Jerry Wilder be retained.

events.title: Jones and Coates square off amid a pizza-party dispute
events.body: The Herald's pre-election issue covered the presidential race between Will Jones and Amanda Coates, alongside a report that SGA was questioning an election-eve pizza party Jones had held, a debate over eliminating the rule requiring a year of SGA experience to run for office, and a heated treasurer's race between Ryan Morrison and Joe Matheis.

events.title: A turbulent election puts Amanda Coates in office
events.body: The Herald's coverage of the spring SGA election was headlined "Turbulent Elections Complete"; the same issue carried an opinion piece, "Student Government Association Offers No Leadership," challenging the incoming administration to prove itself.

events.title: Bill proposes an SGA Information Technology Director
events.body: SGA considered Bill 99-10-F, creating a new SGA position of Information Technology Director.

events.title: Students vote for R&B acts
events.body: SGA ran a student vote on Rhythm & Blues concert programming for campus, reported by the Herald under "Students Vote for R&B."

events.title: Keep our voice: a rally at Wetherby
events.body: About fifty students gathered outside the Wetherby Administration Building to urge the university to retain both the Vice President of Student Affairs and the Dean of Student Life positions, chanting "It's not your choice. Keep our voice." The SGA's own account said president Ransdell appreciated how the students conducted themselves and would keep an open mind.

src.label: WKU SGA site, V.P. of Student Affairs Update (archived 2000)

events.title: Provide-A-Ride in full operation
events.body: During this year SGA ran Provide-A-Ride as a free service giving safe and sober rides anywhere in the Bowling Green and campus area on Thursday and Friday nights from 11 p.m. to 2 a.m. A fifteen-passenger blue van answered calls within about fifteen minutes, and all a rider needed was a valid Western ID.

events.title: The faculty evaluations campaign opens
events.body: President Amanda Coates opened a campaign to publish faculty evaluations as a tool for students choosing professors, starting with a February 22 meeting with the university president and the Faculty Senate chair. The SGA published a step-by-step timeline running through a March 23 presentation to the full Faculty Senate, saying it did not want to win the tool at the expense of unnecessarily upsetting faculty.

events.title: Resolution 00-2-S: publish the evaluations
events.body: Resolution 00-2-S, authored by Amanda J. Coates and Adam Howard and sponsored by the Legislative Research Committee, asked the Faculty Senate to approve a mandatory SGA-sponsored faculty evaluation to be published beginning in fall 2000. Its attached questionnaire asked practical questions such as whether an instructor takes attendance, offers extra credit or gives comprehensive finals.

events.title: Martin and Wright battle to succeed Coates
events.body: The Herald reported that Cassie Martin and Duan Wright were competing to succeed Amanda Coates as SGA president in the spring election.

events.title: Two tickets make their case to succeed Coates
events.body: In the campaign's final week the Herald covered both tickets on the ballot to succeed Coates: Duan Wright with running mate Dwight Campbell, and Cassie Martin with running mate Leslie Bedo, each laying out a platform on the SGA's current issues.

events.title: Martin elected; faculty evaluations move forward
events.body: As Coates's term ended, the Herald's post-election coverage reported Cassie Martin had won the SGA presidency, running an opinion piece titled "Cassie Martin Must Stand Up on Tough Issues," and separately confirmed the SGA-sponsored faculty evaluations Coates's administration had pushed would be conducted and published starting that fall.

events.title: Recount narrows Coates and Martin's win to three votes
events.body: Amanda Coates and running mate Cassie Martin initially led Will Jones and Kara Yeckering 616-611 for president and vice president; after the Coates-Martin ticket asked for a recount to be sure of the win, the recount that night found an even closer margin, 614-611. A write-in ticket of Dwight Campbell and Kerri Richardson finished third with 145 votes. Total turnout was 1,436 students.

events.title: Matheis survives a flier scandal to win vice president of finance
events.body: Joe Matheis defeated Ryan Morrison 700-688 for vice president of finance in the campaign's most contentious race. Two hours after the initial result, SGA's judicial council placed the race under review after fliers Matheis had distributed turned up left on classroom desks and in computer labs overnight, violating election code; the council warned Matheis could lose the seat if he had not made a good-faith effort to collect them. The council let the result stand the next day, and Morrison filed a complaint with the judicial council disputing that decision, saying fliers were still on desks in Garrett and the fine arts center.

events.title: Griffey and Bastin win the remaining executive seats
events.body: Brandon Griffey defeated Amanda Kirby 729-652 for vice president of administration, and Matt Bastin defeated Duan Wright 806-570 for vice president of public relations, completing the 1999-2000 executive slate.

events.title: A letter to the editor questions an SGA probe of racially charged campaign fliers
events.body: A Herald letter to the editor reported that fliers reading "Vote for Will Jones in Racism," written in black ink, had circulated in dorms during the campaign, and that SGA opened an investigation into whether they were racially motivated. The letter's author named Jones - described as the first Black candidate for SGA president in years - as a suspect despite his denial of any involvement, and questioned whether the investigation was following proper procedure rather than targeting him by assumption. No source found reports how, or whether, the investigation was resolved.

events.title: SGA created an Information Technology Director
events.body: Bill 99-10-F created the SGA position of Information Technology Director, and the same month produced a bill amending the constitution to include website guidelines. The association was formalising its web presence as the decade closed.

events.title: A senior awards banquet and hall of distinguished seniors
events.body: Bill 99-5-F established a senior awards banquet and a hall of distinguished seniors, with a companion bill creating an ad hoc committee to run the event. A Meet Your Dean reception bill passed through the same September meetings.

events.title: Congress asked WKU to keep Jerry Wilder
events.body: Resolution 99-1-F requested that Jerry Wilder remain vice president of Student Affairs. The Herald reported the following week that SGA members opposed the move in Student Affairs.

events.title: Topline, a toll-free campus activity line
events.body: Resolution 99-4-F proposed creating a toll-free activity phone line called Topline. The same weeks produced resolutions on WKU banners and suggestion boxes in residence halls.

events.title: Members took the Student Affairs fight public
events.body: The Herald reported that Student Government Association members opposed the administrative move in Student Affairs. The story followed the congress's resolution asking that Vice President Jerry Wilder be retained.

events.title: SGA endorsed ending Flip Friday
events.body: A fall resolution endorsed the schedule proposed by the Class Schedule Review Committee to do away with Flip Friday. It was the association's formal word on one of the era's odder scheduling experiments.

events.title: VarsityBooks.com came to the SGA website
events.body: Bill 99-17-F had SGA join VarsityBooks.com and post a link from its website, and a same-day bill extended library hours during finals week. The dot-com partnership marked the first e-commerce deal in the digitised SGA record.

events.title: SGA proposed its own faculty evaluations
events.body: Resolution 00-2-S proposed creating an SGA faculty evaluation to help students select courses, reviving an idea the congress had pushed since the mid-1990s. It is the last piece of spring 2000 legislation in the digitised collection.

executive.name: Amanda Coates
executive.note: Won a recount, 614-611, over Will Jones and running mate Kara Yeckering.

executive.name: Cassie Martin
executive.note: Coates's running mate; elected SGA president the following year, 2000-01.

executive.name: Joe Matheis
executive.note: Defeated Ryan Morrison 700-688 after surviving a judicial council review over campaign fliers.

executive.name: Brandon Griffey
executive.note: Defeated Amanda Kirby, 729-652.

executive.name: Matt Bastin
executive.note: Defeated Duan Wright, 806-570.

senate.note: Judicial council chief justice John Crowe presided over the election disputes; council member Drew Harvill called the 1999 race the most contentious he had seen. Archive does not preserve a full senate officer or committee list for this year.

documents.title: Herald 74:51, 15 Apr 1999 (election issue)
documents.summary: The College Heights Herald's election-results issue: the front-page report of Amanda Coates's three-vote recount win for president, the full down-ballot results for the other three executive seats, and a letter to the editor questioning SGA's investigation of racially charged campaign fliers.

leaders.name: Cassie Martin
leaders.note: Confirmed against Herald campaign coverage: Rex Hall's series on the Martin-Wright race ran from the candidacy announcement in late March 2000 through an issues debate on the eve of the 13 April 2000 election.
profile: Cassie Martin, a junior from Glasgow, was elected SGA president in April 2000 to lead the association for 2000-2001. With running mate Leslie Bedo, she defeated the ticket of Duan Wright and Dwight Campbell by 654 votes to 541, and the win also made her the student representative on Western's Board of Regents. The race followed weeks of Herald coverage of proposed SGA election-code reforms meant to close loopholes and set spending limits, and the Martin-Wright contest itself was covered from the candidacy announcement in late March through a pre-election issues debate.

Her most visible stand of the year came at the Board of Regents meeting on October 27, 2000, when the board voted 8-2 to raise the student athletic fee by $80 in two installments. Martin was one of only two dissenters, alongside Faculty Regent Mary Ellen Miller. She said she understood the need for the additional funding but questioned the timing and the amount, and disagreed with raising student fees in the middle of an academic year.

SGA's congress in 2001 passed legislation putting $13,000 toward a campus gazebo that was never built. In October 2002 the Herald reported that the money had mistakenly gone back into SGA's general fund and been spent on other things, including computers, and SGA's finance vice president said leaders from the past two years, including former presidents Martin and Leslie Bedo, were all partly responsible for not properly earmarking it.

Cassie Martin, a junior from Glasgow, was elected SGA president in April 2000 to lead the association for 2000-2001. With running mate Leslie Bedo, she defeated the ticket of Duan Wright and Dwight Campbell by 654 votes to 541, and the win also made her the student representative on Western's Board of Regents.

events.title: SGA proposed election code rewrite to close loopholes
events.body: The Herald reported on new Student Government Association election codes intended to close loopholes in how campaigns were run, ahead of the spring 2000 officer elections that Cassie Martin and Leslie Bedo would go on to win.

events.title: Insurance dispute put SGA "on edge"
events.body: The Herald ran a story headlined "Insurance Puts Student Government Association on Edge," in the same issue that covered the ongoing debate over the association's new election codes.

events.title: Election-code debate turned to fairness and spending limits
events.body: The Herald reported that SGA's proposed election codes were meant to ensure fairness between candidates and set campaign spending limits, continuing coverage begun two weeks earlier of loopholes in the existing rules.

events.title: Martin and Wright set to battle for SGA presidency
events.body: The Herald reported that Cassie Martin and Duan Wright would face off for the SGA presidency in the coming spring election, the first coverage of what became the Martin-Bedo versus Wright-Campbell race.

events.title: Martin and Wright discussed the issues on the eve of the vote
events.body: The day before the election, the Herald ran a piece by Rex Hall in which presidential candidates Cassie Martin and Duan Wright discussed the issues facing the campaign.

events.title: Martin-Bedo ticket won SGA presidency
events.body: Students elected Cassie Martin, a junior from Glasgow, as SGA president for 2000-2001, a post that also made her the student representative on Western's Board of Regents. Her ticket with vice presidential candidate Leslie Bedo defeated Duan Wright and Dwight Campbell by 654 votes to 541 in the Thursday election. In the only other contested race, Amy Caswell defeated Billy Lyons 706 to 461 for finance vice president, while Adam Howard and Leslie McClard ran unopposed for the administration and public relations vice presidencies.

events.title: SGA Congress opened its fall 2000 session
events.body: SGA's congress held its first meeting of the fall semester on Tuesday, August 29 at 5 p.m. in Downing University Center room 305. The body met every Tuesday during the semester, and the organization invited students to pick up membership applications in the SGA office on the first floor of DUC.

events.title: Regents raised athletics fee over Martin's dissent
events.body: The Board of Regents voted 8-2 to raise the $16 student athletic fee by $40 in January 2001 and another $40 in fall 2001, to fund a Diddle Arena renovation, a larger football budget for WKU's move to the Gateway Conference, and the athletic department's budget shortfall. Student Regent Cassie Martin and Faculty Regent Mary Ellen Miller cast the two votes against. Martin said she understood the need for the funding but questioned the timing and the amount, and disagreed with raising student fees in the middle of an academic year.

events.title: Bedo ticket stood unopposed to succeed Martin
events.body: SGA's candidate page for the 2001 officer elections listed a single ticket for the top job: executive vice president Leslie Bedo for president with Jamie Sears as her running mate. The only race with two names was for vice president of public relations, between Mark Rawlings and Holly Skidmore, while Aaron Spencer and Jamil Sewell stood alone for the finance and administration vice presidencies. The date shown is the Internet Archive capture date; the page itself carried no date and no results or turnout figures were found in allowed sources.

events.title: SGA planned to conduct and publish faculty evaluations
events.body: The Herald reported that SGA planned to conduct student evaluations of faculty and publish the results starting in fall 2000, in the same issue that covered the close of the Martin-Bedo campaign. The same issue carried an editorial titled "Cassie Martin Must Stand Up on Tough Issues," urging the incoming president to take firmer positions once in office.

events.title: Herald reported SGA membership still declining
events.body: The Herald ran a story headlined "Student Government Association Membership Still Declining," tracking a drop in participation as the Martin administration prepared to take office.

events.title: WKU took student health service back in-house
events.body: WKU announced it would return to self-operation of its campus student health service after its contractor, Collegiate Health Care, notified employees it would be out of business at the end of the day. The university hired the clinic's 17 employees on a temporary basis through the end of the spring semester, and the vice president for Student Affairs promised students would see no reduction in health services.

executive.name: Cassie Martin
executive.note: Also student regent.

executive.name: Leslie Bedo
executive.note: Martin's running mate on the winning ticket.

executive.name: Adam Howard
executive.note: Ran unopposed.

executive.name: Leslie McClard
executive.note: Ran unopposed.

senate.note: Called Congress this year; met weekly on Tuesdays in Downing University Center room 305.

leaders.name: Leslie Bedo
leaders.note: Appears in the WKU Archives regents index marked as student regent for 2001-02 - useful confirmation that by this point president and student regent were the same person.
profile: Leslie Bedo, a senior corporate communications major from Bowling Green, served as SGA president for 2001-02 after three years in the organization, having previously been parliamentarian, public relations committee chair and executive vice president. Her stated priorities for the year were tuition, student health and online course syllabi, and she described SGA as run "by the students, for the students."

As student regent, Bedo pushed back in August 2001 when the Board of Regents raised tuition 9 percent at a meeting held before fall classes officially began. She said the timing sent "a message to students" that the increase would pass before they could weigh in, though she ultimately joined the board's unanimous vote approving it.

That November, Bedo wrote a Herald op-ed titled "Meeting Goals of Student Government Association, But Not Students'", questioning the organization's effectiveness; fellow member Troy Ransdell responded in the same issue with a piece headlined "Action, Not Complaints." The same paper reported SGA was buying Christmas presents for children at Potter Children's Home that season.

In March 2002, near the end of her term, Bedo publicly challenged the university after a land deal meant to add 400 to 500 parking spaces fell through while the Diddle Arena renovation was removing about 200 spaces. She noted regents had raised the student athletics fee on the expectation of more parking, said "the parking has been put on hold," and called added parking imperative because more students parked on campus than attended basketball games.

As her term wound down, an April 30, 2002 Herald profile by Molly O'Connor reported renewed interest in SGA under Bedo's leadership. Jamie Sears was elected to succeed her that April; Bedo's own former rival for vice president of administration, Patti Johnson, went on to become SGA president herself in a September 2004 special election.

events.title: Bedo questions timing of 9 percent tuition increase, then votes for it
events.body: WKU's Board of Regents voted on Friday, August 17 to raise tuition 9 percent starting in fall 2002, the first tuition hike in university history devoted entirely to faculty and staff pay. Student Regent Leslie Bedo said she was troubled that the vote came before students officially began fall classes, telling the board it sent a message that the university would slide the increase through before students could respond. Despite her concerns, Bedo joined the unanimous vote approving the increase, which raised in-state undergraduate tuition $138 a semester, from $1,422 to $1,560.

events.title: Regents approve $32.5 million Diddle Arena bond deal funded by student athletics fee
events.body: The Board of Regents approved an agreement with the City of Bowling Green to sell up to $32.5 million in bonds to renovate E.A. Diddle Arena, with the university repaying the debt service through its student athletics fee. Planned improvements included air conditioning, new seating, luxury boxes, expanded parking and a pedway from new parking areas to the arena. The renovation was scheduled to run from April to September 2002.

events.title: Students organize candlelight vigil after September 11 attacks
events.body: Two days after the September 11 attacks, WKU held a student-organized candlelight vigil at the Ivan Wilson Fine Arts Center Amphitheater as part of a slate of campus responses. The university also planned a faculty forum at Van Meter Auditorium, opened the Faculty House for reflection and counseling, created a condolences message board to send to New York and Washington, and scheduled a blood drive for September 27.

events.title: SGA raises over $800 for Red Cross disaster relief
events.body: The SGA homepage, as archived on November 6, 2001, reported that the association had helped raise more than $800 for the Red Cross Disaster Relief Fund following the September 11 attacks. The same page announced that Congress applications were available in DUC 130 and promoted the Campus Spirit Award, which SGA administered that year.

events.title: Provide-A-Ride carries 929 passengers over twelve fall nights
events.body: SGA's Provide-A-Ride service posted its fall 2001 ridership on its website, listing twelve Thursday and Friday nights of operation between September 20 and November 9, 2001. Nightly passenger counts ranged from 49 to 112, for a total of 929 riders over the period.

events.title: Fall project slate: online syllabi, extended library hours, alcohol policy
events.body: SGA's current-projects page, as archived on November 27, 2001, listed the association's work for the semester. Projects included online course syllabi, extended library hours during finals week, a review of the alcohol policy, a 9/11 Remembrance Wall, the SGA Disaster Relief Fund, Provide-A-Ride keychains, the Senior Class Challenge, the Campus Spirit Award, Homecoming Queen 2001 and the Homecoming parade.

events.title: SGA organized Christmas presents for Potter Children's Home
events.body: The Herald reported that SGA was collecting Christmas presents that fall for children at Potter Children's Home, a Bowling Green residential care facility, in a news piece by staff writer Hollan Holm.

events.title: President Bedo and senator Ransdell publicly debated SGA's effectiveness
events.body: The same Herald issue ran dueling opinion pieces on SGA: an op-ed by President Leslie Bedo headlined "Meeting Goals of Student Government Association, But Not Students'", followed by a response from fellow member Troy Ransdell titled "Action, Not Complaints." The full text of the exchange is not available online; only the headlines and bylines are indexed.

events.title: SGA constitution amended, Spring 2002
events.body: TopSCHOLAR's SGA collection holds a copy of the WKU Student Government Association constitution described as "amended Spring 2002," indicating the association revised its governing document during Bedo's term. The specific amendments are not detailed in the record.

src.label: WKU SGA Constitution, amended Spring 2002, TopSCHOLAR

events.title: Herald profile reported renewed interest in SGA as Bedo's term ended
events.body: With Bedo's term winding down, the Herald ran a profile by Molly O'Connor headlined "Student Government Association President Sees Renewed Interest in Organization." The full article text is not available online; only the headline and byline are indexed.

events.title: Bedo presses parking issue after WKU land purchase collapses
events.body: Negotiations for WKU to buy the Forest Park Trailer Park for 400 to 500 new parking spaces broke down over price, even as the Diddle Arena renovation was set to eliminate about 200 spaces permanently. SGA President Leslie Bedo said several regents had voted to increase the student athletics fee on the basis that student parking would grow, and that the promised parking expansion had been put on hold. She argued more students parked on campus than attended basketball games and called more parking imperative.

events.title: Jamie Sears elected SGA president for 2002-03
events.body: In online voting, junior public relations major Jamie Sears of Melber defeated senior Sam Stinson 1,284 to 594 for SGA president, winning the seat as student representative on the Board of Regents. John Bradley beat Dana Lockhart 1,065 to 730 for executive vice president, Ross Pruitt ran unopposed for vice president of finance with 1,524 votes, Anna Coats edged Holly Skidmore 933 to 809 for vice president of public relations, and Brandon Copeland defeated Patti Johnson 1,106 to 761 for vice president of administration.

events.title: Voters approve Supremacy Clause constitutional amendment
events.body: SGA's official general election results page, archived on April 26, 2002, recorded that a constitutional amendment titled Supremacy Clause passed in the spring 2002 general election. The page listed the amendment result alongside the vote totals for the five executive races.

leaders.name: Jamie Sears
leaders.note: Confirmed in the College Heights Herald's own election headline, which ran the week she won.

sources.label: College Heights Herald 77:51, 11 Apr 2002 - "Jamie Sears Wins Election in Landslide" (O'Connor, Molly)

profile: Sears, a junior public relations major from Melber, won the presidency in a landslide, defeating senior Sam Stinson 1,284 votes to 594 in the April 2002 general election that also seated her incoming executive team: John Bradley as executive vice president, Ross Pruitt as vice president of finance, Anna Coats as vice president of public relations, and Brandon Copeland as vice president of administration.

Sears opened her 2002-03 term as SGA president under immediate scrutiny. Seventeen months after congress passed a bill putting about $5,000 of leftover budget money toward an on-campus gazebo, members discovered the gazebo was never built and the money was gone. When three members petitioned congress in September over $28,000 they said was unaccounted for, Sears told the Herald, "I have absolutely no idea where that money went." The petition was withdrawn only after her executive council created an ad hoc financial review committee.

By October the money had been traced: it had slipped back into SGA's general fund and been spent on other things, including computers for the SGA office. Sears acknowledged that she and former student activities director Scott Taylor had decided during the summer where the leftover money, which included the gazebo funds, would be allocated, saying other executive council members were consulted through email. She said the financial review committee would explain the budget findings to congress, and no move was made to set aside new gazebo money.

Sears finished the year on stronger footing. She traveled with about 20 Western students to Frankfort to oppose state budget cuts to higher education, calling the trip one of SGA's greatest accomplishments: "That was a great feeling seeing students from everywhere rallying for the same cause." Under her leadership congress debated more than 55 pieces of legislation and passed the first student referendum in SGA history, a $3 fee for radio station Revolution 91.7 that students approved in the spring election. Her final meeting as president came on April 22, 2003.

events.title: Record enrollment of 17,500 strains campus
events.body: Western opened the fall with enrollment ballooning to 17,500, nearly 1,000 more students than the year before and a 20 percent increase since 1997. President Gary Ransdell warned that growth would be "painful" amid decreased state funding, and the Board of Regents approved a 10.4 percent tuition increase for 2003-04.

events.title: Members demand answers on missing gazebo money
events.body: SGA members Brooke Smith, Dana Lockhart and Sam Stinson petitioned congress over $28,000 they said was unaccounted for, including about $5,000 that a April 2001 bill had set aside to build an on-campus gazebo that never appeared. President Jamie Sears said of the gazebo fund, "I have absolutely no idea where that money went." The petition was withdrawn after the executive council formed an ad hoc financial review committee.

events.title: Herald editorial blasts SGA over 'Gazebo-Gate'
events.body: The Herald's 11-member editorial board attacked SGA leaders over what it called "Gazebo-Gate," saying the money had gone to computers for the SGA office instead of the promised gazebo. It called leaders' ignorance about the missing money "shameful" and challenged Sears by name to "do her job" and provide real answers, writing that "I don't know" did not cut it.

events.title: Gazebo funds traced to SGA general fund
events.body: Vice president of finance Ross Pruitt reported that the $13,000 SGA had put toward the gazebo mistakenly went back into the organization's general fund and was spent on other things, including computers for SGA. Sears said she and former student activities director Scott Taylor decided over the summer where the leftover budget money would go, with other executive council members consulted by email. Pruitt said leaders from the past two administrations shared the blame, saying "I didn't do my homework."

events.title: Congress votes down enrollment cap resolution
events.body: SGA congress rejected by a large margin a resolution asking Western to implement an enrollment cap, with Sears among those calling the measure too drastic. The failed proposal argued the university and state budgets had not kept pace with enrollment growth from 14,543 students in 1997 to about 17,770. Provost Barbara Burch and President Ransdell both said a cap was not the best answer to the growth problem.

events.title: Three resolutions pass on faculty pay, enrollment, parking
events.body: SGA passed two resolutions responding to a shortage of 75 faculty members and the lowest-paid faculty in the state, asking that unbudgeted tuition surplus money, about $800,000 that year, be used to hire faculty, and encouraging President Ransdell to create a task force on enrollment. A third resolution requested a change to the policy that gave Hilltopper Athletic Foundation donors student parking spaces, including the Grise Hall lot, at basketball games.

events.title: Freshman committee appointments tabled
events.body: SGA tabled Sears's proposal to appoint three freshmen, Tim Howard, Katie Dawson and Robert Watkins, as the student members of a joint University Senate and SGA enrollment growth committee. Sears said she picked freshmen so they could serve the committee's expected two to three year life, but critics including associate justice Dana Lockhart said the appointments would make it hard for SGA to be taken seriously.

events.title: SGA joins Frankfort rally against budget cuts
events.body: About 200 students from six public universities rallied at the state Capitol against cuts to higher education, after the Kentucky House passed a budget cutting Western's funding by more than $1 million. Western sent a delegation of roughly 20 people including SGA members, organized through the board of Kentucky's student body presidents. Sears said 17 people "took the initiative to get on the bus."

events.title: Congress puts $3 radio fee referendum on ballot
events.body: SGA unanimously approved a bill placing a referendum on the April 2-3 general election ballot letting students vote on a $3 student fee for campus radio station Revolution 91.7-WWHR, which was operating on a $7,000 budget unchanged since 1998. Executive vice president John Bradley, who championed the measure, said it would empower students and boost voter turnout. A yes vote would send the fee recommendation to the Board of Regents for a final decision.

events.title: Bradley elected president; 2,014 vote
events.body: A total of 2,014 students voted in the spring SGA election, with results announced shortly after 1 a.m. Friday by chief justice Holly Skidmore. Paducah junior John Bradley won the presidency unopposed with 1,662 votes, Patti Johnson beat Dana Lockhart 1,185 to 685 for executive vice president, and Jessica Martin beat Shawn Peavie 1,056 to 686 for vice president of administration. The $3 WWHR radio fee referendum passed 1,066 to 765 and moved to the Board of Regents.

events.title: SGA closes year after 55 pieces of legislation
events.body: SGA held its last meeting of the year on April 22, having heard and debated more than 55 pieces of legislation, including a resolution that earmarked funds for new benches across campus. Sears counted the Frankfort rally among the year's greatest accomplishments, and the Revolution 91.7 fee measure stood as the first student referendum in SGA history, awaiting a final Board of Regents vote on May 9. President-elect Bradley said the high election turnout was the semester's best moment and pledged to fight student apathy the next year.

executive.name: John Bradley
executive.note: Championed the WWHR radio-fee referendum; elected SGA president for 2003-04.

senate.note: No senate officer or committee roster for 2002-03 could be confirmed. TopSCHOLAR holds weekly meeting-minutes abstracts for this year (Aug 2002-Apr 2003, e.g. digitalcommons.wku.edu/sga/Meetings/Minutes/), but the full-text PDFs return an automated bot challenge that this run could not clear; abstracts alone name agenda topics (committee vacancies discussed 9 Oct 2002) without naming chairs. The ad hoc financial review committee formed in the gazebo-funds dispute is the only committee identified by name in confirmed sources.

leaders.name: John Bradley
leaders.note: Presided over the 2004 Constitutional Convention that created the three-branch structure. Quoted in Herald coverage of the investigation into his successor-elect.
profile: Bradley, a Paducah junior and sitting executive vice president, ran unopposed for SGA president in spring 2003, campaigning alongside Jessica Martin and Dana Lockhart on parking, keeping the cost of education low and making campus friendlier to students with disabilities. He counted the WWHR radio-fee student referendum among his accomplishments as executive vice president, and said he had worked to "depolarize the organization." As president he would also serve as the student member of the Board of Regents.

He opened the fall 2003 semester by naming low education costs his top priority, opposing plans to pass Greek Village land costs on to all students, and steering SGA toward campus safety after serving on the summer's Campus Safety Task Force. He launched an SGA Ambassador Council to visit student organizations weekly and scheduled the semester's first forum on campus safety.

events.title: The Constitutional Convention rebuilds the body
events.body: Three branches - Executive Cabinet, Senate and Judicial Council - drawn from the student body at large. The most consequential clause is the quietest: every enrolled student became a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections.

events.title: The president-elect is investigated before he takes office
events.body: The Herald reported an investigation into missing funds from an SGA dining account. Articles of impeachment were drafted against the president-elect's existing finance post but the judicial council found the two-week process could not finish before the term ended. Because state law governs the student regent seat, the new constitution required a separate special election to fill it.

events.title: Bradley opens the year with cost, safety and involvement goals
events.body: New SGA president John Bradley opened the fall by naming low education costs his first goal and warning that fees for the proposed Greek Village should not be passed to the whole student body. SGA created an Ambassador Council to visit student organizations weekly, and planned its first forum of the semester on campus safety, an issue Bradley had worked on as a member of the Campus Safety Task Force formed after the death of freshman Katie Autry. The first congress meeting of the semester was set for August 26 in Downing University Center.

events.title: SGA lines up against plus/minus grading
events.body: SGA members voiced concern at their Tuesday meeting over a plus/minus grading system proposed in the University Senate by economics professor Brian Strow. Bradley said he planned to oppose it, reporting that the state's other student body presidents had urged him to fight it, and the Academic Affairs committee prepared a student questionnaire on the change. Chief Justice Troy Ransdell argued the system would penalize students who scored best.

events.title: Congress urges students to vote as grading petition circulates
events.body: SGA unanimously passed a resolution recommending that Western students vote in the November 4 state election and research the candidates' stands on higher education, suspending the bylaws so it could pass before the vote. Members also reported that the petition against plus/minus grading had gathered 350 signatures with more petitions in circulation, and SGA planned a Homecoming tent on the Downing University Center south lawn.

events.title: SGA organizes for a higher education rally in Frankfort
events.body: SGA prepared to join student governments from across Kentucky at a February 5 rally at the state Capitol against cuts to higher education funding, with slogans such as "Don't Balance the Budget on Our Backs" and students asked to wear backpacks. Congress approved $650 for transportation and reserved 47 spots for the trip. Bradley conceded change that year might be "unreasonable" to expect but said rallying could affect the future.

events.title: SGA budget frozen as Western absorbs $5.6 million in cuts
events.body: SGA announced at its Tuesday meeting that its budget, along with the Campus Activities Board's, had been informally frozen while Western worked out how to cut $5.6 million ordered by Gov. Ernie Fletcher's administration. SGA held $65,309.52 in its 2003-04 budget at the time, plus about $7,400 in an Aramark contract and foundation accounts that were not affected. Bradley said congress could still pass legislation requiring money, with the director of student activities deciding whether funds were available.

events.title: Nick Todd elected SGA president as 1,232 students vote
events.body: Vice president of finance Nick Todd won the SGA presidency with 772 votes to Jessica Martin's 424, in a two-day online election in which 1,232 students voted. Katie Dawson won executive vice president with 778 votes and Evelina Petkova won administrative vice president with 692, with the first elected senate under the new constitution chosen at the same time. Bradley said he was disappointed by the turnout, and the winners were set to be sworn in at the SGA banquet on April 27.

events.title: Congress buys stepping stones for muddy campus paths
events.body: SGA unanimously approved legislation allocating $200 from its campus improvements account for stepping stones near Mass Media and Technology Hall, Tate Page Hall and Southwest Hall, where student foot traffic had worn dirt and mud paths. The bill's authors, Shawn Peavie and Sarah Cecil, said sidewalks had been considered but were too expensive. In the same meeting a straw poll on a proposed dorm Internet service fee drew 3 votes in support, 11 against and 11 abstentions.

events.title: SGA races to spend its remaining $45,000
events.body: With about $45,000 left of its original $105,000 budget for 2003-04, SGA moved to spend the remainder before the semester ended, since leftover funds would go to offset budget cuts across the university rather than carry over. Officers attributed the surplus partly to frugality during the spring budget freeze, and Todd suggested putting the money toward campus improvements such as benches or shuttle shelters. SGA also sponsored a dining services forum that week with Auxiliary Services and Dining Services officials.

events.title: Disputed 9-8 vote clouds the first speaker of the senate election
events.body: Congress elected constitution author Robert Watkins as the first speaker of the senate by 9 votes to 8 over Brittany Fausey, with 17 of 20 members present voting. The result was immediately questioned because the new constitution was unclear on whether two-thirds of eligible voters or of total membership was required, and three members present were barred from voting under a judicial council ruling. Martin warned of a "semester of frustration" if the dispute was not resolved at the year's final meeting, while Fausey declined to challenge the result.

leaders.name: Patti Johnson
leaders.note: Confirmed: president-elect Nick Todd resigned in July 2004 amid a dining-funds investigation; Johnson, the sitting executive vice president, ran unopposed in the September 2004 special election and was sworn in Sept. 23, matching the plaque year. A Board of Regents resolution read into the 22 Jul 2005 minutes confirms she served as the board's student member from August 2004 to July 2005, when Katie Dawson was sworn in to replace her.

sources.label: WKU Board of Regents minutes, 22 Jul 2005 (TopSCHOLAR)

profile: Patti Johnson, a senior from Marion, had been active in SGA for over three years and served on committees including public relations and athletics before becoming executive vice president in 2003-04. Nick Todd, the vice president of finance, was elected president for 2004-05 in March 2004, but before the new officers were sworn in on April 27, SGA's judicial council fielded an allegation that $611 was missing from the SGA Dining Dollars account, an account that had started the year with $5,000. Senator Josh Collins drafted articles of impeachment against Todd's vice presidency, but the judicial council ruled a two-week impeachment process could not finish before he left that office anyway. Johnson had not planned to run for president herself, but after Todd's resignation that July she entered the September 2004 special election as the only candidate to show interest, saying she stayed on because of "the turmoil within the organization" and that she knew "what it takes to get the job done."

Johnson ran unopposed for president and student regent in the Sept. 14-15 online election, the group having been without an elected president since July. She said she was disappointed that students would not "really get to make a decision," but still planned light campaigning, and she wanted to continue reviewing the plus/minus grading proposal and to make faculty evaluations available to students.

Johnson received 1,291 votes in the two-day uncontested election and was sworn in as president at SGA's fall reception on Sept. 23, 2004, one week after her election. She said committees had been formed and members had begun proposing legislation, and she looked forward to being sworn in as student regent at the Oct. 29 Board of Regents meeting, declaring it was "back to business." She served through the year until Katie Dawson was elected to succeed her in the March 2005 spring election.

Johnson served as the Board of Regents' student member from August 2004 to July 2005, a term confirmed by the resolution of appreciation the board read into its July 22, 2005 minutes when Katie Dawson, the executive vice president who had served alongside her all year, was sworn in to replace her. Dawson had come up through the cabinet as Todd's running mate in the original March 2004 election and had acted as interim president during the summer vacancy before Johnson's win.

Patti Johnson, a senior from Marion, had been active in SGA for over three years and served on committees including public relations and athletics before becoming executive vice president in 2003-04. She had not planned to run for president, but after Nick Todd's resignation she entered the September 2004 special election as the only candidate to show interest, saying she stayed on because of "the turmoil within the organization" and that she knew "what it takes to get the job done."

events.title: SGA president Nick Todd resigned amid funds investigation
events.body: Nick Todd, elected SGA president in March with 772 of 1,232 votes cast, submitted his resignation in July, citing personal conflicts within the association. The former vice president of finance had come under investigation in April for the misuse of more than $600 in an SGA Dining Dollars account. Executive Vice President Katie Dawson acted as president until a new election set for Sept. 14-15.

events.title: Internal audit recommended Todd repay SGA money
events.body: WKU's Office of the Internal Auditor reported that $872 in questionable purchases were made from the SGA Dining Dollars account between August 2003 and May 2004, mostly small buys at campus restaurants with no receipts. The report recommended that Todd reimburse the money, plus $71 for a charge made with the SGA purchasing card after a spring break car rental. Campus police determined no police action was necessary.

events.title: Patti Johnson emerged as the only candidate in the special election
events.body: At a meeting for students interested in running in SGA's September special elections, Marion senior Patti Johnson, the previous year's executive vice president, was the only student to show interest in the presidency. She said she decided to run because of "the turmoil within the organization." Applications were also taken for the 23 open senate seats ahead of online voting on Sept. 14-15.

events.title: Dean of Student Life contradicted Todd on sanctions
events.body: Howard Bailey, dean of Student Life, said Todd had been sanctioned by judicial affairs in July over the alleged misuse of university funds, disputing Todd's public claim that losing access to the Dining Dollars card was the only action taken against him. Bailey said federal privacy law barred him from revealing the sanctions. Todd acknowledged he was also no longer allowed to handle any SGA funds.

events.title: SGA approved a $110,000 budget
events.body: SGA approved a $110,000 budget for the 2004-05 academic year, up from $105,000 the year before, despite earlier expectations of a $15,000 to $17,000 cut under the university's budget reduction plan. Most of the money went toward operating fees, campus improvements and organizational aid. Adviser Charley Pride credited steady enrollment growth for the increase.

events.title: Johnson sworn in as president after winning 1,291 votes
events.body: Patti Johnson was sworn in as SGA president at the organization's fall reception on Sept. 23, after receiving 1,291 votes in the uncontested online election held Sept. 14 and 15. The 23 new senators were seated in the first fall senate election held under SGA's new constitution. Johnson was due to be sworn in as student regent at the Oct. 29 Board of Regents meeting.

events.title: SGA proposed a faculty evaluation pilot to the University Senate
events.body: SGA prepared to propose a two-year pilot program to the University Senate that would add five questions on matters such as office hours, punctuality and textbook use to faculty evaluations and post the answers on TopNet for students. Senator Josh Collins wrote the proposal with Troy Ransdell and Morgan Phelps after SGA scaled back an earlier push to release entire evaluations. The questions could appear on evaluations at the end of spring 2005 if the study was approved.

events.title: Katie Dawson elected SGA president for 2005-06
events.body: Executive Vice President Katie Dawson defeated Senate Speaker Josh Collins 1,268 to 472 in the spring election's only contested race to become the next SGA president. Students also passed a package of 40 constitutional amendments 1,193 to 262 and voted 1,019 to 669 to ask the Board of Regents to institute a $9 per semester Talisman yearbook fee. Mason Stevenson and Melissa Paris won the two vice presidencies unopposed, and all 25 senate candidates on the ballot were elected.

events.title: SGA funded the Buy-A-Book program
events.body: SGA passed legislation 22-2 on April 5 allocating $2,000 to the Buy-A-Book program, and the University Bookstore pledged to match the amount. The bill by senator Katharine Pettit was amended unanimously to help 20 students who needed financial assistance buying textbooks instead of 10. Recipients were to be chosen by the academic affairs committee based on a required essay and need.

events.title: Goodrum found not guilty in Katie Autry murder trial
events.body: A jury in Owensboro found Lucas Goodrum, 23, of Scottsville not guilty of the May 2003 murder of Pellville freshman Melissa "Katie" Autry, who was set on fire in her Poland Hall dorm room and died three days later. The verdict came March 21 after three hours of deliberation, ending a three-week trial that had been moved from Warren County. Stephen Soules had earlier pleaded guilty to murder, rape, sodomy, arson and robbery and expected life in prison.

events.title: SGA judicial council fielded impeachment bid against president-elect Todd
events.body: Days before new officers were due to be sworn in on April 27, SGA's judicial council found that $611 was missing from the SGA Aramark Dining Dollars account, which had started the academic year with $5,000 and had about $1,200 left. Senator Josh Collins drafted articles of impeachment against Todd's outgoing vice presidency of finance, but the council ruled a two-week impeachment process could not be completed before he left that office regardless. Only Todd, outgoing president John Bradley and adviser Charley Pride held cards to the account.

executive.name: Patti Johnson
executive.note: Also held the Board of Regents' student seat from August 2004 to July 2005.

src.label: WKU Board of Regents minutes, 22 Jul 2005 (TopSCHOLAR)

executive.name: Katie Dawson
executive.note: Elected Todd's running mate in March 2004; acted as interim president during the summer 2004 vacancy and continued as Johnson's EVP through the year before winning the presidency herself for 2005-06.

senate.note: Senator Josh Collins, who had drafted the spring 2004 impeachment articles against Nick Todd, was still serving that fall when he co-wrote the faculty-evaluation proposal with Troy Ransdell and Morgan Phelps. Senator Katharine Pettit sponsored the spring 2005 Buy-A-Book bill. No senate officer or committee-chair list survives in the sources found so far.

leaders.name: Katie Dawson
leaders.note: Named in April 2004 Herald coverage as incoming executive vice president, so she came up through the cabinet. Confirmed as a 2005 presidential candidate in College Heights Herald election coverage, and the paper's own election-night story names her as the winner.

sources.label: College Heights Herald 80:38, 24 Feb 2005 - "Two Announce Plans to Run for Student Government Association President - Katie Dawson, Josh Collins" (Coulter, Amber)

profile: Dawson served as both SGA president and student regent during Western's centennial year. When the university launched its 14-month centennial celebration on Nov. 19, 2005, she spoke at the dedication of Centennial Plaza, offering her own meaning for the school slogan: "Find what you love and carry it with you your whole life through."

Her spring semester was dominated by a proposed $46-per-semester fee for three campus construction projects. At a student forum with President Gary Ransdell she suggested exempting the next year's seniors, who would graduate before any project was finished; the Board of Regents rejected the exemption 10-1 at its April 7 meeting and approved the fee 9-1. Dawson cast the lone abstention, saying that although she supported the fee, she could not vote for it with so many seniors counting on the exemption.

Her term ended at Western's 159th commencement on May 13, 2006, where the Radcliff native graduated with a degree in corporate and organizational communication and addressed her 1,797 fellow undergraduates as SGA president. She charged the graduates to have courage, endurance, strength, patience and character, saying success was knowing "when to throw in the towel and when to wave it around and cheer."

events.title: The plus/minus grading fight
events.body: An Institutional Research report on plus and minus grading, a protest broadside, a post-winter-term student survey and an SGA handbook all survive - one of the few academic-policy campaigns documented from research through to public agitation.

events.title: WKU launched its centennial celebration
events.body: Western kicked off a 14-month celebration of its 1906 founding on Saturday, Nov. 19, dedicating three new campus landmarks including Centennial Plaza. SGA President Katie Dawson spoke at the plaza dedication, offering her own meaning of the school slogan "The Spirit Makes the Master."

events.title: SGA closed the fall with 10 pieces of legislation
events.body: The Herald reported that SGA passed 10 pieces of legislation in the fall semester, fewer than in previous fall semesters. Its legislation brought bikes, a cancer documentary and iPods to Western. The same issue reported that a senator named Johnson had been elected the new speaker of the senate.

events.title: SGA took up a proposed $45 construction fee
events.body: At its first regular meeting of the spring semester, SGA discussed a proposed $45-per-semester fee to pay for a campus-wide wireless network, a new health center and renovations to the Ivan Wilson Center for Fine Arts. President Katie Dawson supported the fee, and Western's chief financial officer estimated it would raise about $1.4 million a year.

events.title: Ransdell asked SGA for a resolution backing the fee
events.body: WKU President Gary Ransdell came to the SGA meeting and urged senators to pass a resolution supporting the proposed $45 fee, which the Board of Regents would vote on April 7. Dawson sat on that board as student regent, and SGA officers said a supporting resolution was likely within a few weeks.

events.title: Executive vice president aired an internal rift
events.body: Executive Vice President Mason Stevenson read a letter at the SGA meeting saying some members trying to protect their political interests had "thwarted" SGA's mission to improve Western. The letter outlined his concerns about relations between the executive and legislative branches.

events.title: Senate put $2,000 toward SGA's 40th anniversary party
events.body: Two bills devoting $2,000 to a party for SGA's 40th anniversary passed unanimously at the group's Tuesday meeting. The Herald reported the organization planned a campus-wide party to mark four decades of student government at Western.

events.title: Regents approved the fee; Dawson's senior exemption failed
events.body: The Board of Regents voted 9-1 to approve the $46-per-semester construction fee, with Dawson abstaining, and rejected 10-1 her proposal to exempt next year's seniors, an idea she had raised at a student forum the week before. Dawson said that although she supported the fee, she could not vote for it with so many seniors counting on the exemption.

events.title: Rob Watkins elected SGA president
events.body: Bowling Green senior Robert Watkins won the online election for SGA president after spending more than a week seeking supporters who would vote on TopNet. He defeated Berea junior Kara Ratliff, and the results were announced Tuesday at a crowded Revolution 91.

events.title: Executive board issued its first veto of the year
events.body: After the Tuesday senate meeting, the SGA executive board vetoed a bill that would have financed community- and campus-oriented projects through civic engagement grants, the first time it exercised its veto power that year. The Herald reported the grants were "a reality for only about 30 minutes" and that time restraints halted an appeal of the veto.

events.title: Herald editorial attacked SGA misspending
events.body: A Herald editorial titled "SGA misspending" said members should not have to be "motivated by a giveaway to show up for meetings." It noted that the opinion page had devoted considerable space in recent weeks to both positive and negative aspects of SGA, which it said could and should be an important organization on campus.

executive.name: Mason Stevenson
executive.note: Read a letter to the March 2006 SGA meeting airing a rift between the executive and legislative branches.

executive.name: Melissa Paris
executive.note: Office not further specified in the election coverage; won unopposed alongside Stevenson.

senate.note: All 25 senate candidates on the March 2005 ballot ran unopposed and were elected. A senator surnamed Johnson was reported elected speaker of the senate in December 2005, but no source found gives a first name, so the office is left unfilled here rather than guessed.

leaders.name: Robert Watkins
leaders.note: Single-year plate and the only name attached to 2006 because Watkins resigned partway through the 2006-07 term; no plate covers the full year. Confirmed against Herald election coverage: a Bowling Green senior, he won the SGA presidency in the 13 April 2006 online election, defeating Berea junior Kara Ratliff. He had been elected the first speaker of the senate under the new constitution on 15 April 2004, a result contested 9-8 and then upheld. He resigned as president and student regent on 28 November 2006, per SGA's own senate minutes for that day's regularly scheduled Tuesday meeting, which record the resignation being read into the record; this site previously followed a Herald account giving the date as 30 November, which this run corrects against the primary minutes.
