leaders.name: Will Harris
leaders.note: From Glasgow. Sworn in as student regent 2 August 2019. His term ran into the March 2020 campus shutdown.

sources.label: WKU News - regents swear in student regent

profile: Harris won the student body presidency in April 2019 at the head of the WGK ticket with Garrett Edmonds and Kenan Mujkanovic, defeating Asha McWilliams. After the results were announced at SGA's election party, he said he looked forward to "making a positive impact for all students here at WKU" and to collaborating with the opposing ticket. He took office at SGA's annual banquet and presided over his first meeting the following Tuesday.

The defining controversy of his fall semester was Resolution 4-19-F, the senate's push to punish Alpha Xi Delta after a video showed members singing a racial slur. Harris abstained when his executive board vetoed the resolution 4-0, explaining that the discrimination claim would have to come from the Student Code of Conduct and that no violation had been noted by the Office of Student Conduct. When senators suggested his position as a knight of Alpha Xi Delta motivated him, he rejected the charge and said he wanted to reach an amicable outcome with the resolution's authors.

events.title: Harris-led WGK ticket wins SGA executive election
events.body: The WGK ticket of Will Harris, Garrett Edmonds and Kenan Mujkanovic won the spring SGA elections, with Harris defeating Asha McWilliams for student body president. Edmonds was re-elected to a second term as executive vice president and Mujkanovic defeated Symone Whalin for administrative vice president. Results were announced at SGA's election party, with the new officers set to take office at the annual banquet; the Herald's results story reported no turnout figures.

events.title: First meeting of the year confirms five executive appointments
events.body: At its first official meeting of the semester, the senate confirmed all five of President Will Harris's executive branch nominees: Aubrey Kelley as chief of staff, Ashlynn Evans as chief of public relations, Abbey Norvell as director of academic and student affairs, Paul Brosky as director of information technology and Josh Zaczek as Legislative Research Committee chair. Appointees outlined plans including wider use of counseling center fee vouchers and a revival of the need-based Earn-a-Computer program.

events.title: Senate blocks budget over special projects fund
events.body: The senate refused to pass the year's budget over a $6,500 special projects fund the executive branch wanted for a sand volleyball court and hammock space at the First Year Village green space. Senators including Anthony Survance objected that the allocation cut into scholarship money, with Survance calling the motion "slimy", and the senate voted to keep $3,000 in its discretionary fund and $35,000 in scholarships. The executive branch pulled the budget, forcing a week's wait before a revised version could be voted on.

events.title: Budget passes unanimously with spending stipulations
events.body: All 13 senators approved the yearly budget after a compromise added stipulations restricting the special projects fund to the First Year Village plans and redistributing any money unspent by March 3 back to discretionary and voucher funds. The budget's passage let Bills 1-19-F (Greeks Go Green) and 2-19-F (funding for Bowling Green Pride) pass unanimously. The senate also amended its election codes to halve campaign spending maximums, which had been $300 for presidential candidates, $125 for vice presidential candidates and $50 for senate candidates.

events.title: Senate passes Resolution 4-19-F against Alpha Xi Delta
events.body: The senate voted 24-7 to pass Resolution 4-19-F, authored by senators Symone Whalin and Anthony Survance, supporting disciplinary action up to suspension from Greek affairs against the Epsilon Kappa chapter of Alpha Xi Delta. The resolution followed an August Twitter video showing AXiD members singing a racial slur in a rap song, and the authors said administrative silence signaled the university did not care about minority students. Before passage the senate amended the title to drop a call for outright removal from campus.

events.title: Executive board veto of Resolution 4-19-F upheld
events.body: The executive board vetoed Resolution 4-19-F by a 4-0 vote with two abstentions, and the senate confirmed the veto at its Tuesday meeting. President Will Harris, one of the abstainers, said the resolution's discrimination claim would have to come from the Student Code of Conduct and no violation had been noted by the Office of Student Conduct, while co-author Anthony Survance accused the executive branch of dragging the issue out. Senators also raised Harris's connection to Alpha Xi Delta as one of its knights, which he rejected as grounds for bias.

events.title: Go With the Flow feminine hygiene bill passes unanimously
events.body: Bill 1-20-S, funding the Go With the Flow program that supplies feminine hygiene products in campus restrooms, passed the senate unanimously. The bill, carried forward by Campus Improvement Chair Matthew Barr, doubled the program's budget from $588, and a floor amendment from Senator Symone Whalin raised the final amount to $1,300 from senate discretionary funds. Products were to be placed in Grise Hall, DSU, Preston Center, Gary Ransdell Hall and Snell Hall, including gender neutral bathrooms.

events.title: Senate approves $5,000 hammocks project
events.body: The senate voted to pass Bill 3-20-S, allocating $5,000 from the special projects fund to begin planning hammock poles across campus, after the sand volleyball court proposed earlier in the year was deemed too expensive. Planned locations included spots near most residence halls and the Valley, and Executive Vice President Garrett Edmonds said he and Harris ran so SGA would be known for more than "scantrons and greenbooks". Legislative Research Chair Josh Zaczek criticized having to vote without seeing budget numbers, and the senate retained power to halt spending during planning.

events.title: WKU extends spring break, moves classes online amid COVID-19
events.body: WKU announced it would extend spring break by one week and transition to "alternative delivery formats" for classes amid growing coronavirus concerns, with President Tim Caboni recommending that students who could safely return home do so. The announcement came after the University of Kentucky and University of Louisville suspended in-person classes. In-person instruction never resumed that semester, upending the rest of SGA's spring calendar.

events.title: Spring elections postponed until fall as SGA moves to Zoom
events.body: With campus closed by COVID-19, SGA postponed its spring elections until at least September so voting could happen in person, and added an "emergency clause" constitutional amendment allowing cabinet terms to be extended until the following election with judicial oversight. The cabinet continued meeting over Zoom every Tuesday. Harris said that after scholarships were awarded, the remainder of SGA's budget would be donated to the WKU Opportunity Fund and Emergency Relief Fund, and SGA gave its remaining food bank goods to the Office of Sustainability for redistribution.

leaders.name: J. Garrett Edmonds
leaders.note: The COVID year. Almost certainly the most unusual term in the organisation's history and worth a dedicated oral history.
profile: Edmonds, a senior from Island, Kentucky, spent his freshman year as chair of the Campus Improvements Committee, working with Vice President of Student Affairs Brian Kuster on projects including a campus safety walk, before winning election as executive vice president in April 2018 on a ticket with Harper Anderson and Stephen Mayer. He served two years as executive vice president under President Will Harris, pushing for a budget model geared toward campus amenities and recreational life and working to diversify Senate appointments with seats for underrepresented students.

He ran for the presidency in fall 2020 on the Edmonds-Norvell ticket, after his original running mate for administrative vice president, Nathan Terrell, dropped out and was replaced by Abbey Norvell. The campaign centered on a pledge to create a Director of Outreach position to close the communication gap between campus organizations and SGA, and the Sept. 24 Herald town hall covered WKU's COVID-19 response and the summer's Black Lives Matter protests on campus. Voting ran Sept. 28-29 on TopNet; Edmonds defeated senator MJ Mayo, becoming SGA president and, since the two offices had merged by then, student regent on the WKU Board of Regents. Norvell was elected administrative vice president alongside him, with the Herald reporting no decision yet made on a separate executive vice president post.

Taking office amid the pandemic, the senate confirmed Isaac Keller to a vice-president post 29-1 in October after Edmonds said he wanted a deputy willing to challenge him; the Herald's report on that vote first called the office executive vice president, then ran a correction changing it to administrative vice president -- the same title the Herald had given Norvell in September, a conflict the record does not resolve. Matt Barr, Ashlynn Evans, Kody Okert and Paul Brosky rounded out the executive and Shelby Robertson served as non-voting speaker of the senate. Early cabinet business set up officer office hours, an ad hoc outreach committee chaired by Me'Lon Craighead and a push toward inclusive pronoun language in Senate proceedings. That fall SGA petitioned WKU to restore Pass/D/Fail grading for COVID-disrupted students; Associate Provost Rob Hale initially rebuffed the request, calling the university's extended drop deadline sufficient, but by December the petition -- more than 3,500 signatures in three days -- had succeeded, and Edmonds thanked senators for the work behind it at the semester's final meeting alongside bills funding campus safe-driving signage and several student organizations.

In the spring his senate passed the organization's largest-ever organizational aid bill and a resolution seeking a codified vetting process for campus dining vendors after a controversial social media post by a local pizzeria owner, alongside legislation backing WKU's Naming and Symbols Task Force in renaming buildings tied to racism, a community garden, and a diversity-event push by DEI chair Fatin Yaro. Near the end of his term he declined to fill the chief justice seat vacated by Erika Puhakka, saying the choice belonged to his successor: "I think that's the only thing that is right in this scenario." He also worried publicly that only 13 students were running for senate in the April election, and closed his term addressing the Class of 2021 at the delayed Fall 2020/Spring 2021 commencement, telling graduates their perseverance through "this past year" had brought them to their day of celebration.

events.title: Town hall debate pitted the sitting EVP against a senator
events.body: SGA held a town hall debate in the DSU auditorium between presidential candidates Garrett Edmonds, the sitting executive vice president, and senator MJ Mayo. Edmonds's original running mate for administrative vice president, Nathan Terrell, had dropped off the Edmonds-Norvell ticket and was replaced by Abbey Norvell; the debate covered WKU's COVID-19 response and the summer's Black Lives Matter protests on campus.

events.title: Edmonds elected president over Mayo
events.body: Garrett Edmonds, the sitting executive vice president, was elected student body president over senator MJ Mayo in balloting held on TopNet Sept. 28-29, succeeding Will Harris. Edmonds had campaigned on creating a Director of Outreach position to link campus organizations more directly with SGA.

events.title: Senate passed the annual budget 28-5 and elected Shelby Robertson speaker
events.body: At the first official senate meeting under the new leadership, Shelby Robertson defeated Brenna Matthews to become speaker of the senate and the budget passed 28-5. Edmonds emphasized a $6,000 Projects Fund, including $1,000 for Housing and Residence Life PPE and an expansion of the Go with the Flow menstrual products program into Pearce Ford Tower. Senator MJ Mayo challenged the balance of stipends; Edmonds said all senate stipends except the top three offices had been cut to feed the Projects Fund.

events.title: Cabinet set office hours, an outreach committee, and pushed inclusive language
events.body: At the executive cabinet's first recorded meeting, Edmonds set up officer office hours and an ad hoc outreach committee for RSO leadership. Speaker Shelby Robertson pushed to connect senators with similar legislative interests, adopt inclusive pronoun language in the chamber, and find a parliamentarian.

events.title: Keller confirmed AVP 29-1; two new committee chairs elected
events.body: The senate confirmed Isaac Keller as administrative vice president 29-1 after Edmonds said he wanted a deputy willing to challenge him when they disagreed. Roderick Maul and Tess Welch were elected committee chairs, and senators voted to form a new Ad Hoc committee chaired by Me'Lon Craighead.

events.title: Presidential task force sought input on slaveholding college namesakes
events.body: WKU's Presidential Task Force on Naming and Symbols, formed by President Timothy Caboni in fall 2020, collected input from students and the community on the namesakes of Potter College and Ogden College, both built on wealth from slave labor. Two Potter descendants said it was time to find a new name. The task force planned to audit names and send recommendations to the administration.

events.title: SGA backed renaming buildings tied to racism and funded a community garden
events.body: The senate passed legislation by Brenna Matthews and Tess Welch offering SGA's support to the Naming and Symbols Task Force in changing the names of WKU buildings with ties to racism or injustice. Matthews said ties to slave owning and the Confederate army did not belong on a campus committed to diversity. Senators also unanimously funded a community garden outside the Office of Sustainability and allocated $3,500 to four student organizations.

events.title: Largest organizational aid bill passed; chief justice resigned before elections
events.body: Edmonds announced that Chief Justice Erika Puhakka had stepped down and declined to nominate a replacement so close to elections, and warned that only 13 people were running for senate. The senate passed its largest organizational aid bill ever, funding five student groups, and passed 16-0 with two abstentions a bill by Kyle Phillips asking WKU to support a codified vetting process for campus dining vendors after a controversial social media post by the owner of Lost River Pizza.

events.title: WKU relented and allowed pass grades after SGA's P/D/F campaign
events.body: Provost Cheryl Stevens told faculty that students who faced COVID-related problems could opt for a pass grade instead of a B or C, reversing the university's earlier refusal. The Faculty Senate had voted 40-9 in favor and SGA voted unanimously for the option, presenting nearly 20 pages of student testimony; SGA's petition had drawn over 3,500 signatures in three days. Students had to email their professor by Jan. 13, with the final decision left to the faculty member.

events.title: Edmonds addressed the Class of 2021 at the delayed commencement
events.body: As SGA president, Edmonds spoke at WKU's Fall 2020/Spring 2021 commencement ceremony, telling graduates that the class's perseverance through the pandemic year had brought them to their day of celebration.

events.title: Norvell elected administrative vice president; EVP still open
events.body: SGA held a virtual election party over Zoom to announce results. The Edmonds-Norvell ticket defeated MJ Mayo for the presidency, and Abbey Norvell was elected administrative vice president alongside Edmonds. The Herald reported no official decision had yet been made on a separate executive vice president post, with an announcement expected at the next SGA meeting.

events.title: Judicial nominations confirmed; senate revives a Pass/D/Fail request
events.body: The senate unanimously confirmed Edmonds's nominations of Derek Collins and Lexi Mayne as associate justices and Addison McCoun as senator at large. Senators passed a Tess Welch/Eric Barry bill to increase campus accessibility and split funding for SGA-branded masks and hand sanitizer between the senate and SGA's PR team. A closing bill by Tate McClard and Jacob Congleton, with every senator listed as a co-author, asked WKU to restore the Pass/D/Fail grading option it had offered in spring 2020 but declined to bring back that fall.

events.title: Edmonds launched a P/D/F petition
events.body: President Garrett Edmonds released a student petition asking WKU to offer a Pass/D/Fail grading option for the fall semester, citing inconsistent course modalities and the strain of quarantine on students without an online-learning fallback. The petition reached half its 1,000-signature goal within an hour and the target was raised to 5,000.

events.title: Associate provost rebuffed SGA's P/D/F request; computers bill passes 28-3
events.body: Edmonds told senators that Associate Provost Rob Hale had defended the university's decision to extend the drop deadline rather than restore Pass/D/Fail grading, and said he was "deeply disturbed" by the response; senator Brenna Mathews argued the policy left students choosing between attending in person or paying for an extra semester. Edmonds urged senators to keep circulating his petition, which had passed 3,000 signatures, and the senate voted 28-3 to fund recycled computers for the SGA office, a number scaled back to meet CDC guidelines.

events.title: Fall semester closed with a safe-driving pledge and organization funding
events.body: At the last meeting of the fall semester, Edmonds thanked senators for the work that led to the new P/D/F option. Senators unanimously passed a Matthew Thomas bill committing SGA's social media to a "Drive Safe Hilltoppers" safety campaign, and unanimously funded a bill supporting HonorsToppers, College Republicans, Zeta Phi Beta and the Sociology and Criminology Club.

events.title: Spring semester opened over Zoom with a late-fee pledge
events.body: At its first meeting of the spring semester, held on Zoom, SGA heard Edmonds say the provost search was in its final stage with interviews starting within weeks, and that he planned to look at changing or removing the late fees charged when a student's financial aid arrives late. Senators unanimously nominated Jamison Moorehead as director of IT and funded Dance Big Red and a Delta Sigma Pi virtual leadership conference.

events.title: Committee chairs set spring priorities
events.body: Legislative Research Chair Dawson McCoun said the shift to remote meetings after March 2020 had made it harder to connect with students and pass legislation. Diversity and Inclusion Chair Fatin Yaro announced a Feb. 24 diversity event and legislation to set consequences for discrimination within student organizations, and Chief of Staff Matt Barr said he would continue the "Go with the Flow" program installing free menstrual-product dispensers on campus. SGA planned a return to masked, socially distanced in-person meetings that semester.

events.title: New senator seated; rally with Gov. Beshear announced
events.body: SGA nominated pre-law sophomore Will Dykeman as a new senator and Edmonds announced a virtual Student Body President rally for March 26 featuring Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, with Edmonds working to add state Rep. Charles Booker. Senators unanimously funded a bill by AVP Isaac Keller supporting Amazing Tones of Joy, Black Women of Western, Queer Student Union and the Business Association for Development, and voted $2,500 for ISEC's Black Magic Masquerade Ball on a bill by Me'Lon Craighead.

events.title: Outreach signage and safe-driving bills pass
events.body: Guest speaker Ethan Logan, vice president of enrollment and student experience, briefed senators on how his office could help SGA. Edmonds pointed senators toward an upcoming provost-search update and urged them to consider running in the April officer elections. Senators unanimously passed a Me'Lon Craighead bill funding 50 laminated, QR-coded outreach signs for campus and a Matthew Thomas bill adding 12 safe-driving signs to campus parking lots; a bill on WKU's Naming and Symbols Task Force was held for the following week.

events.title: Constitution amended; Caboni's contract extended
events.body: Edmonds told senators the WKU Board of Regents had extended President Timothy Caboni's contract four years. The senate elected Addison McCoun to head the Legislative Research Committee after Dawson McCoun's resignation, passed a Tess Welch/Erika Puhakka bill amending constitutional wording 19-4, and funded a Sustainability Committee spring photo contest on a bill by Matthew Waninger and Elizabeth DeLozier.

documents.title: SGA Executive Cabinet minutes, 13 October 2020
documents.summary: Minutes from the first recorded fall 2020 executive cabinet meeting under President Garrett Edmonds, covering officer office hours, an ad hoc outreach committee, and Speaker Shelby Robertson's push for inclusive language and a parliamentarian.
documents.extract: Ad hoc committee for outreach; inclusive language in senate; looking for a parliamentarian.

src.label: WKU SGA Executive Cabinet Minutes, 13 Oct 2020

executive.name: J. Garrett Edmonds
executive.note: Also student regent on the WKU Board of Regents.

executive.name: Isaac Keller
executive.note: Confirmed by the senate 29-1 on 20 Oct 2020. The Herald's report on this vote originally called the post executive vice president and ran a correction changing it to administrative vice president -- the same title the Herald's 30 Sep 2020 election story gives to Abbey Norvell, elected AVP alongside Edmonds. Sourcing does not resolve which title is correct.

executive.name: Abbey Norvell
executive.note: Elected on the Edmonds ticket 29 Sep 2020. The Herald's election story used the same 'administrative vice president' title later given (after a correction) to Isaac Keller, confirmed by the senate that October; the conflict between the two Herald reports is unresolved. As of the 30 Sep 2020 story, no decision had been made on a separate executive vice president post.

committees.name: Ad Hoc (Outreach)
committees.note: Formed October 2020.

committees.name: Diversity and Inclusion Committee
committees.note: Held a diversity event 24 Feb 2021 and pursued legislation on organizational discrimination consequences.

committees.name: Legislative Research Committee
committees.note: McCoun resigned in March 2021; Addison McCoun was elected to succeed him 18 Mar 2021.

senate.note: Cabinet also included Matt Barr, Ashlynn Evans, Kody Okert and Paul Brosky; Roderick Maul and Tess Welch were elected committee chairs in October 2020 (SGA Executive Cabinet minutes, 13 Oct 2020, https://www.wku.edu/sga/executive/execs_minutes/sga_execminutes_10_13_20.pdf). Roderick Maul and Tess Welch were also elected general committee chairs in October 2020; Me'Lon Craighead chaired the Ad Hoc/Outreach committee. Speaker Shelby Robertson announced full committee rosters by Zoom breakout room at the 20 Oct 2020 meeting.

leaders.name: Matthew Wininger
leaders.note: Sworn in as student regent 6 August 2021, at the meeting that renamed Northeast Hall for Margaret Munday, WKU's first African American student to enrol.
profile: Wininger ran for student body president in the April 2021 SGA election, with voting held on TopNet April 12-13. In the Herald's ballot guide he said he wanted to make SGA "the most active and vibrant organization on campus." Me'Lon Craighead, who would serve as his executive vice president, ran for that office in the same election.

As president, Wininger opened the fall semester by welcoming new and returning senators to the second meeting of the 21st Senate. He presided over the unanimous confirmation of senators elected the previous semester and of his executive appointments, including Jamison Moorehead as IT director, Alexis Courtenay as public relations director and Parker Raybourne as chief of staff, and the senate adopted new election codes at the same meeting.

In spring 2022 Wininger welcomed senators back from winter break and announced an initiative to create a student resource handbook aimed particularly at underclassmen, encouraging all SGA committees to pitch in on the project. At that same first meeting of 2022, the senate he led responded to the December tornado disaster by unanimously passing a $1,000 bill to restock the Office of Sustainability food pantry.

events.title: Northeast Hall renamed for Margaret Munday
events.body: Student Regent Matthew Wininger was sworn in at the Board of Regents meeting that renamed Northeast Hall for WKU's first African American student to enrol - the first building on campus named after an African American.

events.title: Cole Bornefeld elected with 49% of 1,448 votes
events.body: Alexis Courtenay took 40% and Olivia Feck 11%. Sam Kurtz and Garrison Reed were elected to the two vice presidencies.

events.title: SGA opened the fall term with confirmations and new election codes
events.body: SGA held its first meeting of the fall semester, the second meeting of the 21st Senate, with President Matthew Wininger welcoming new and returning senators. All senators present were confirmed by unanimous consent and sworn in by Chief Justice Holden Schroeder, along with executive appointments Jamison Moorehead as IT director, Alexis Courtenay as public relations director and Parker Raybourne as chief of staff. New election codes for the next semester also passed with unanimous consent.

events.title: Senate confirmed the year's budget
events.body: At the third meeting of the 21st Senate on Sept. 7, SGA passed Bill 1.21f, confirming its budget for the year. Dean of Students Martha Sales spoke on leadership, and Wininger announced a planned donor drive in partnership with at least four other student organizations. Chief of Staff Parker Raybourne announced a Hilltopper Hangout event for Sept. 24.

events.title: New senators seated and freshman election results announced
events.body: The senate unanimously voted in four new senate members, two judicial council members and Trib Singh as director of academic and student affairs. Speaker of the Senate Tess Welch introduced committees on legislative operations, student experience, mental health, sustainability, campus improvement, diversity and student outreach. That night the fall election results named Addison Falkner, Sam Kurtz and Jenna Wells freshman senators and Arivumani Srivastava the Gatton Academy senator.

events.title: 21st Senate passed its first resolution, on advisor evaluations
events.body: At its Oct. 5 meeting SGA passed Resolution 1.21f, addressing the lack of an advisor evaluation system, by a 21-2 vote, the first resolution of the 21st Senate. Bill 2.21f, barring the speaker of the senate from voting on legislation, passed 21-2, and two bills scrubbing outdated 2007-era bylaws passed by unanimous consent. Parking director Jennifer Tougas discussed a possible monthly parking tag subscription and campus bookstore operations.

events.title: Resolution condemning critical race theory bans passed 16-15
events.body: After weeks of debate, the senate passed Resolution 7.21f, which condemned the banning of critical race theory teachings in postsecondary education ahead of an anticipated bill in the Kentucky legislature. The vote was 16 in favor, 15 against, with two abstentions. Sponsor Olivia Blackmon said the measure was meant to ensure intellectual freedom in the curriculum.

events.title: EF-3 tornado struck Bowling Green, killing 11 in Warren County
events.body: An EF-3 tornado with 150 mph winds slammed into Bowling Green early on Dec. 11, killing 11 people according to the coroner and destroying homes and businesses across Warren County. Gov. Andy Beshear signed a state of emergency and President Biden signed an emergency declaration. The disaster shaped SGA relief efforts the following semester.

events.title: First 2022 meeting funded tornado-drained food pantry
events.body: At its first meeting of 2022, SGA passed Bill 1.22s by unanimous consent, providing $1,000 to restock the WKU Office of Sustainability food pantry, whose food and toiletries had been drained by the tornado recovery effort. Wininger announced an initiative to create a student resource handbook for underclassmen. Speaker Tess Welch announced spring election dates of April 18-19.

events.title: Syllabi clause, crosswalk resolutions and Title IX meetings passed
events.body: At its Feb. 15 meeting SGA unanimously passed Resolution 6-22-S to add an SGA-related clause to course syllabi, which the Herald reported would be the first of its kind in SGA history. Three resolutions supported new crosswalks below the Van Meter green space and on Chestnut and Normal streets, and Bill 6-22-S required a committee chair or delegate to meet with the Counseling Center director and Title IX coordinator each semester. The senate also approved a task force for the iWKU app and funding for a financial success workshop.

events.title: Judiciary Council cleared Bornefeld's campaign over student-all email
events.body: After several SGA members complained that presidential candidate Cole Bornefeld's student-wide email about the Swipe Out Hunger initiative violated the election code's ban on self-promotion, the Judiciary Council held a roughly hour-long Zoom hearing on April 13 and voted in favor of his campaign. Speaker Tess Welch argued the signed email constituted self-promotion, while a statement from President Wininger, read by Chief Justice Holden Schroeder, said nothing in the code required executive approval for a student-all email. Senators said the initiative saw a record number of donations after the email went out.

events.title: End-of-year allocations funded scholarships, organizational aid and planetarium donation
events.body: Hours before the 2022 election results were announced, the senate passed a slate of funding bills: $8,000 in organizational aid at $500 per applicant, and $15,500 across five scholarship programs including summer class, study abroad, ISEC book and Scholar Level scholarships, plus $500 to Black Student Alliance scholarships for the first time. The senate also approved $325 for the Hardin Planetarium, $500 for a student worker appreciation event, $300 for the CEC Run/Walk for Autism and $570.02 for an e-waste recycling bin on main campus.

leaders.name: Cole Bornefeld
leaders.note: Elected April 2022 with 49% of 1,448 votes. In February 2023 the Speaker of the Senate brought a censure case against him over anti-transgender posts he had liked on Instagram; the Judicial Council voted unanimously against censure, and a Title IX report seeking his removal was filed two days later. Last name currently on the plaque.
profile: Cole Bornefeld came to the presidency by an unusually fast route. He transferred to WKU from Volunteer State Community College as a junior, emailed then-President Matthew Wininger during his first week on campus, and was appointed a senator-at-large at their first meeting. He had not planned to run for president, but after senators urged him to, he formed a ticket the week of the filing deadline and won. He campaigned on programs he backed as a senator, including the Share-A-Swipe meal donation program and growing SGA's scholarship budget, which rose by $3,500 during his presidency. Adjusting to the office, he said it felt like "drinking out of a fire hose," and he sought advice from former student body presidents weekly.

Bornefeld opened the 2022-23 year with an executive retreat on Aug. 29 at the Cliff Todd Center, where his team set three priorities: a one-stop resource guide for students, a push to represent WKU's five regional campuses, which he said was "an area that I really don't think SGA has ever touched," and financial assistance for students as the year's underlying goal. He had met with the director of regional campuses the week before to start that work.

His spring semester was dominated by fallout from anti-LGBTQ Instagram posts he had liked. After the judicial council unanimously declined to censure him, the Queer Student Union removed SGA meetings from its list of campus safe spaces and said it would not associate with SGA until a public apology was released. Addressing the senate on Feb. 21, Bornefeld, who also served as student regent, said he "always commits to loving thy neighbor" but could not commit to always agreeing, tying his position to his Christian values and offering to meet any student over coffee or breakfast to discuss disagreements.

events.title: The Speaker takes the President to the Judicial Council
events.body: Speaker of the Senate Yulia 'Julie' Mishchuk requested a censure hearing against President Cole Bornefeld over anti-transgender posts he had liked on Instagram. Members of the Queer Student Union and both vice presidents attended. The Judicial Council voted unanimously against censure.

events.title: A Title IX report seeks the President's removal
events.body: Filed with Student Conduct. Under the constitution, removing an executive who will not resign requires written endorsement from at least 20% of the Senate, a wait of at least fourteen days and a two-thirds vote of the full Senate sitting as a court.

events.title: Sam Kurtz elected on an unopposed ticket
events.body: With Salvador Leon as administrative vice president and Annalise Finch as executive vice president.

events.title: Executive retreat set the year's goals
events.body: SGA's executive team held a formal retreat dinner on Aug. 29 at the Cliff Todd Center to set its agenda for the year. President Cole Bornefeld said the group was building a one-stop resource guide for students and trying to promote SGA at WKU's regional campuses in Elizabethtown, Fort Knox, Glasgow, Owensboro and Somerset. Speaker Julie Mishchuk said the underlying goal of the year was financial assistance for students.

events.title: First meeting filled senate and cabinet vacancies
events.body: At its first meeting of the year on Aug. 30, the senate approved all of President Bornefeld's nominees, including Juan Thomas, Will Hemenover and Sydney Denney as senators-at-large, Aniya Johnson as director of information technology, Donte' Reed as director of enrollment and student experience, and Isaac Kind and Garrett Baum to the judicial council. Administrative Vice President Sam Kurtz spoke on the budget and Chief Justice Holden Schroeder swore in the new members.

events.title: Fall election turnout doubled; Reed appointed to state council
events.body: Fall 2022 election results announced at midnight seated Rush Robinson, Callison Padgett and Rhett Helland as freshman senators, plus Neel Patel for Gatton Academy, Shy'Ante Williams as graduate senator and Salvador Leon Golib as international student senator. President Bornefeld said the vote total rose from 398 the previous fall to 805. SGA also announced that Vice President Garrison Reed had been appointed student representative on Kentucky's Council on Postsecondary Education, with a term running through June 30, 2023.

events.title: Senate approved five nominations and reviewed a shrinking budget
events.body: The senate unanimously confirmed five nominations, including Adan Canizalez as chair of student enrollment and experience and Miles Huff, a track athlete, to the judicial council. Administrative Vice President Sam Kurtz urged senators to sponsor more resolutions, which use university funds, because only about $39,460.76 remained of SGA's $100,000 annual budget for bills. Speaker Julie Mishchuk floated a constitutional amendment requiring every senator to sponsor at least one bill or resolution.

events.title: Voucher bills funded dental clinic, ID center and Preston Center
events.body: The senate unanimously passed Bill 28-23-S, putting $500 toward free teeth cleanings at the WKU Dental Health Clinic after voucher use rose 660 percent in the fall, and Bill 27-23-S, allocating $2,000 in discount vouchers split 60/30/10 among the Preston Center, the ID center and the dental hygiene clinic. A $260 bill funding a poetry mic night with the Talisman also passed with one nay vote. Former SGA President Matthew Wininger opened the meeting as guest speaker.

events.title: Narcan resolution aimed to put overdose spray in residence halls
events.body: SGA unanimously passed Resolution 2-23-S on Feb. 7 supporting placement of Narcan, an opioid overdose reversal spray, in WKU residence halls. SGA had planned to spend about $1,000 of its own budget, but a University of Kentucky harm reduction specialist helped secure the product through a government grant instead. Housing and Residence Life planned to install the spray in AED-style boxes across its 15 dorms by Aug. 1 to allow time for staff training.

events.title: Menstrual product legislation passed as QSU protested
events.body: At its Feb. 21 meeting SGA passed a resolution supporting menstrual product dispensers on the first floor of every academic building, a $200 bill to distribute 35 menstrual cups at tabling events, and $100 for a community relations survey. Queer Student Union president Alistar Flowers announced QSU had removed SGA meetings from its list of campus safe spaces after the judicial council declined to censure President Bornefeld, and said QSU would not associate with SGA until a public apology was released.

events.title: Election reform bill failed 19-15
events.body: Bill 39-23-S, which would have moved the transfer, non-traditional and first-generation senate seats to the fall election and required a two-thirds senate vote to convert vacant seats to at-large seats, failed 19-15, short of the two-thirds needed. Sponsor Neel Patel called the growing reliance on presidential appointments a dangerous practice for a government organization. The same meeting unanimously funded the April 3 Afro-Latinidad cultural event and rejected funding for Dance Big Red.

events.title: Senate merged committees and funded Mental Health Awareness Week
events.body: At the April 11 meeting the senate passed Bill 44-23-S, a constitutional amendment merging the Community Relations and Outreach committees starting in 2023-24, which Speaker Mishchuk said would create a stronger committee amid low membership. Senators also unanimously funded a slate of Mental Health Awareness Week events for April 23 through 28, including an Out of the Darkness suicide prevention walk, and passed a $62 terrarium tabling bill. President Bornefeld reported 44 applicants for the upcoming SGA elections.

events.title: WKU dedicated the Commons at Helm Library
events.body: WKU formally dedicated the $35 million Commons at Helm Library, a renovation funded through a partnership with Aramark, and President Timothy Caboni announced early plans for a similar makeover of Cherry Hall. SGA President Cole Bornefeld spoke at the ceremony, saying the building had been full of excitement and community since it opened.

leaders.name: Sam Kurtz
leaders.note: Former administrative vice president. Elected April 2023 on an unopposed ticket with Salvador Leon and Annalise Finch.
profile: Sam Kurtz, then the outgoing administrative vice president, was elected student body president in results announced early on April 19, 2023 in the Downing Student Union senate chambers, after voting opened on TopNet on April 17. His KFL ticket, with Annalise Finch as executive vice president and Salvador León as administrative vice president, ran unopposed, and Chief Justice Justin Goins read the results. In a statement, Kurtz said the ticket would "listen to students' concerns, represent their voices, lead with integrity, and promote transparency."

At the 23rd Senate's first fall meeting on Aug. 29, Kurtz nominated Ashley Ranger, Anna Kate Hardin, Ellen Henderson, Morgan Gammons and Garrison Reed to the Judicial Council from what he called a record number of applicants, and named seven committee heads, including Rush Robinson for Campus Improvements and Sustainability and Karley Solorzano for Diversity, Equity and Inclusion. The Senate's first bill of the year, passed unanimously that September, funded the SGA Pink Walk breast-cancer event. That November the senate backed moving DSU fire drills from 5 a.m. to 2 a.m. and funded a Boys and Girls Club toy drive. Speaker of the Senate Sydney Denney wrote or co-wrote several of the year's bills, including a resolution capping student parking fees at $50, a $700 fund to help students pay parking fines, and voucher funding for the Dental Hygiene Center and ID Center. In February 2024 Kurtz and Chief of Staff Donté Reed rolled out a 450-voucher Uber giveaway aimed at student safety and outreach, followed in March by a need-based scholarship awarding Uber vouchers and a Community Builder Excellence Scholarship for incoming Bowling Green-area freshmen; that month the senate also planned a Frankfort trip for the Rally for Higher Education.

The year's fight was internal. In February 2024 the Judicial Council voted 6-0 to censure Administrative Vice President Salvador León after a hearing brought by Denney and the executive cabinet, which alleged León had spent SGA funds - including a $425.25 Preston Center deposit for Neurodiversity Acceptance Week - before the Senate passed the funding bill, in violation of the constitution's clause 2.5.3 requiring the administrative vice president to expend funds only as the Senate authorizes. Chief Justice Isaac King said the cabinet, excluding León, had asked for the censure after León spent the funds despite Kurtz's condition that he wait for Bill 22-23-F to pass, and after he pushed PR Director Preston Romanov to promote the week on SGA social media ahead of the vote, effectively forcing the Senate's hand. León countered that text messages showed Kurtz had signed off on the spending in advance; the council found the spending improper but recommended no discipline beyond the censure itself.

In January 2024 Chief of Staff Lindsey Kelly and enrollment director Donte Reed both resigned, with Reed moving up to chief of staff. That April, Kurtz ran for a second term with Reed as his executive vice president candidate and junior senator Ethan Taylor for administrative vice president; the ticket again ran unopposed on a ballot of more than 60 legislative candidates, and the three were re-elected as the 24th Senate's 34 members were announced the night of April 16-17, 2024. Before that, SGA partnered with WKU Red Wave for a final Red Wave tailgate on April 9, with a student-DJ contest winner earning a $500 scholarship. The 23rd Senate held its last meeting on April 16 with no legislation on the agenda, and Kurtz thanked senators in his final report for what the group had accomplished that year.

events.title: The 23rd Senate corrects its own governing documents
events.body: Three bills from the Legislative Operations Committee: fix references to a 'University Senate' that had since split into separate Faculty and Staff senates, reconcile bylaws language about expelling senators with a constitution that only provides for impeachment, and update committee names that had drifted.

events.title: 23rd Senate seats Judicial Council and committee heads
events.body: At its first meeting of the fall semester, SGA approved President Sam Kurtz's nominations of Ashley Ranger, Anna Kate Hardin, Ellen Henderson, Morgan Gammons and Garrison Reed to the 2023-2024 Judicial Council after what Kurtz called a record number of applicants. Kurtz also announced seven committee heads, including Rush Robinson for Campus Improvements and Sustainability and Karley Solorzano for Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion. The new appointees took the oath of office at the meeting.

events.title: First bill of the year funds the Pink Walk
events.body: The 23rd Senate passed its first piece of legislation, Bill 1-23-F, at its fifth meeting. The bill allocated $500 from SGA's scholarship budget for the SGA Pink Walk, an October breast cancer awareness event for students and the Bowling Green community. It passed unanimously with 28 votes.

events.title: Fall election winners sworn in
events.body: SGA announced its fall election results on Sept. 20 over an Instagram livestream, electing Savanna Kurtz, Malick Ibrahim and Chloe Ralston as freshman senators, ShyAntye'e Williams as graduate senator, Sim Guan Zhou as international senator and Livi Ray as Gatton Academy senator. Five of the six were sworn in at the following Tuesday meeting. Sophomore senator Rush Robinson received the year's first Senator of the Month award.

events.title: Midyear resignations reshuffle the executive cabinet
events.body: President Sam Kurtz announced the resignations of Chief of Staff Lindsey Kelly and of Donte Reed as director of enrollment and student experience. The senate approved Kurtz's nominations of Reed as the new chief of staff and Sarah Vincent as director of enrollment and student activities. Kurtz also filled vacant transfer/non-traditional, sophomore and graduate senate seats with Sawyer Edmonds, Gabe Jerdon and Elizabeth Gannon.

events.title: Judicial council censures Salvador León
events.body: The SGA judicial council voted 6-0 to censure Administrative Vice President Salvador León after a Feb. 7 hearing on allegations that he spent funds, including a $425.25 Preston Center deposit for Neurodiversity Acceptance Week, before the senate passed the funding bill. León argued text messages showed President Sam Kurtz had accepted the spending, while Kurtz said he asked León multiple times not to spend before the bill passed. The council recommended no further disciplinary action beyond the censure.

events.title: Uber voucher program and parking fee measures
events.body: President Sam Kurtz and Chief of Staff Donte Reed announced a program of 450 Uber vouchers worth $10 each, distributed through social media giveaways, meeting attendance and SGA events. The senate also passed Resolution 18-23-S supporting a cap on student parking fees at $50 and Bill 19-23-S allocating $700 to help financially vulnerable students pay parking fines, along with $1,045 in Dental Hygiene Center and ID Center vouchers.

events.title: Funding for DEI Week and Spring Fling
events.body: At its 20th meeting the senate funded SGA Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Week, four days of themed tabling from March 25 to 28 covering mental health, campus demographics, sexual health and deaf awareness. A $450 bill for the SGA Spring Fling, whose proceeds went to the Kids Cancer Alliance, passed 28-2 after debate among senators over the amount being spent. A $280 bill funded a Hope Harbor Denim Day event for Sexual Assault Prevention Month.

events.title: 23rd Senate holds its final meeting
events.body: The 23rd Senate met for the last time with no legislation on the agenda, spending the meeting on senators' final remarks. Kurtz thanked the senate and said in his final report, "We've done a lot of great things this year." Executive Vice President Annie Finch and Administrative Vice President Salvador León also gave closing reports before the 24th Senate's first meeting on April 23.

events.title: Kurtz re-elected unopposed to a second term
events.body: Running with Chief of Staff Donté Reed for executive vice president and junior senator Ethan Taylor for administrative vice president, Kurtz was re-elected without opposition as the 24th Senate's 34 members were announced the same night. More than 60 students had appeared on the ballot for the spring 2024 general election.

events.title: Senate backs a later fire-drill time, funds a toy drive
events.body: At the 23rd Senate's 11th meeting, senators unanimously passed Resolution 6-23-F, backing a change to DSU fire-drill timing from 5 a.m. to 2 a.m. after the Mental Health and Wellness Committee argued the earlier hour caused sleep problems and anxiety for students on early schedules or with accommodations. They also unanimously passed Bill 12-23-F, allocating $200 from the legislative discretionary fund for a Boys and Girls Club of Bowling Green toy drive, and swore in newly elected ISEC senator Ashlee Potter.

events.title: Spring committee heads sworn in
events.body: At the spring semester's first meeting, Kurtz appointed Madison Parker Payne as Outreach Committee chair and Sophia Bryant as Mental Health and Well-Being Committee chair; both were approved without contested debate. Executive Vice President Annalise Finch appointed Jaden Marshall to chair the Graduate Advisory Council campus committee and Chloe Ralston to chair the Colonnade General Education committee. Kurtz urged senators to spend down the senate's still-large discretionary budget before the semester's end.

events.title: Cabinet requests censure hearing against León
events.body: Kurtz told the senate the Executive Cabinet had filed a formal report seeking a Judicial Council censure hearing against Administrative Vice President Salvador León. Chief Justice Isaac King said the cabinet's complaint was that León spent project funds before President Kurtz or EVP Finch consented, that he had done so after Kurtz conditioned permission on Bill 22-23-F first passing, and that he pushed PR Director Preston Romanov to promote Neurodiversity Week on SGA social media before the funding bill passed, effectively forcing the Senate's hand. The Executive Cabinet, excluding León, asked for a censure; the hearing was set for Feb. 7.

events.title: Rally trip to Frankfort, new voucher and cleanup plans
events.body: Kurtz previewed a senate trip to Frankfort for the Rally for Higher Education, where SGA planned to meet state Rep. Kevin Jackson and other Kentucky campus governments, and urged senators to seek re-election to preserve institutional knowledge. Chief of Staff Donté Reed introduced a need-based scholarship awarding four Uber vouchers and the Community Builder Excellence Scholarship for incoming Bowling Green-area freshmen. Campus Improvements and Sustainability chair Rush Robinson moved Earth Day from April 22 to April 19 and set a tentative Bowling Green cleanup for March 28.

events.title: SGA closed the year with a Red Wave tailgate
events.body: SGA partnered with WKU Red Wave for the school year's last tailgate before a baseball game against Louisville, featuring winners of a "Battle of the DJs" social-media poll; sophomore Wilson Patterson won the $500 top scholarship prize as "DJ WLZN." Kurtz called the crowd to "savor one last tailgate of the 2023-2024 school year," with SGA grilling food for attendees.

events.title: Spring general election opened with over 60 candidates
events.body: Voting for the spring 2024 general election opened on TopNet with more than 60 students on the ballot for legislative seats. Kurtz, Chief of Staff Donté Reed and junior senator Ethan Taylor ran unopposed for student body president, executive vice president and administrative vice president respectively; the legislative council ballot included three senior, three junior and three sophomore senator seats, six college seats, an ISEC senator, a first-generation senator, a transfer/non-traditional senator and 14 senator-at-large seats.

documents.title: SGA Constitution, as amended for 2023-2024
documents.summary: The governing constitution posted for Kurtz's first term, defining the executive, legislative and judicial branches and their duties.
documents.extract: Clause 2.5.3: the Administrative Vice President shall "Expend funds as authorized by the Senate."

executive.name: Salvador León
executive.note: Censured 6-0 by the Judicial Council on 7 Feb 2024 over premature spending.

committees.name: Student Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee

senate.note: The 2023-2024 Judicial Council was Ashley Ranger, Anna Kate Hardin, Ellen Henderson, Morgan Gammons and Garrison Reed, nominated by Kurtz from a 'record number' of applicants (Herald, 30 Aug 2023). Justin Goins, chief justice of the outgoing Judicial Council, read the April 2023 election results. Isaac King is confirmed as chief justice by 6 Feb 2024, explaining the Executive Cabinet's censure complaint against León (Herald, 6 Feb 2024), and was still chief justice at the April 2024 town hall; exactly when he succeeded Goins between Aug 2023 and Feb 2024 is not established in available sourcing.

leaders.name: Sam Kurtz
leaders.note: Re-elected unopposed. Warned the Senate repeatedly that an unusually senior chamber meant the 2025 election mattered more than usual.
profile: Kurtz opened the 2024-25 year presiding over the 24th Senate, which passed SGA's $100,000 budget at its first meeting on Aug. 27. Sitting down with the Herald editorial board alongside his executive cabinet, he described SGA as "a vessel for good" and a group of 45 to 50 people advocating for students, and credited President Caboni with keeping the budget untouched for several years.

Through the spring he presided over a run of student-welfare legislation, including the Gordon Wilson Hall elevator resolution and a resolution seeking 24/7 library hours during finals week. In February he announced a POLLapalooza push to raise election participation, telling the Senate, "My goal is that 3,000 students vote in our election."

Kurtz closed his term at the 24th Senate's final meeting on April 15, having served as student body president for two years and holding executive branch positions for most of his college career, and prepared to graduate at the end of the semester. He received a standing ovation after his last report, and his parting words to senators were "Please be for the students."

events.title: A mental health survey, and a warning about the election
events.body: The Senate passed Bill 4-25-S funding a DEI Committee tabling event to gather anonymous mental health survey responses. Dean of Students Martha Sales told the Senate 'you cannot isolate and educate at the same time'. Kurtz warned repeatedly that an unusually senior chamber made the spring election matter more than usual.

events.title: Rush Robinson elected on a turnout of 966
events.body: Elected alongside class, college, transfer, first-generation, Intercultural Student Engagement Center and Honors College senators - constituencies the 1966 constitution had no concept of.

events.title: Senate passed $100,000 budget at first meeting
events.body: At its first meeting of the year on Aug. 27, the SGA Senate passed a $100,000 budget for 2024-25, including $20,000 for organizational aid, $23,500 for scholarships and $10,705 in legislative discretionary funding. Executive leaders told the Herald editorial board they intended to spend the full allocation, and President Sam Kurtz credited WKU President Caboni with keeping the budget level for several years.

events.title: Fall election winners sworn in, school safety bill passed
events.body: Five senators elected in the fall election, three freshman senators plus an international and a Gatton Academy senator, were sworn in at the Oct. 1 meeting. The Senate passed three bills, including Bill 4-24-F to make school safety training mandatory for WKU professors and require posted emergency exits in classrooms, and two bills backing a Spooktober fundraiser for the Potter Children's Home Initiative.

events.title: Three senators removed for excessive absences
events.body: Senators Malick Ibrahim, Myricle Gholston and Karisha Petty were removed from their seats at a Nov. 6 censure meeting after each accumulated at least six unexcused absences from weekly senate meetings. The Judicial Council voted 7-0 to remove them under a constitutional provision requiring removal of any senator censured twice, calling the decision a matter of accountability rather than an attack on character.

events.title: Trump DEI order prompted constitutional review
events.body: Chief Justice Morgan Gammons said the SGA Constitution might require amendment to its diversity, equity and inclusion provisions after President Trump's executive order directing federal agencies to end DEI mandates. Gammons said the Judicial Council would meet to decide whether an amendment was needed, noting that WKU receives federal funding as a public university. The Senate also filled several appointed positions at the same meeting.

events.title: Resolution backed Gordon Wilson Hall elevator
events.body: The Senate passed Resolution 2-25-S supporting installation of elevators in Gordon Wilson Hall, prompted by wheelchair user Kiersten Washington, whose dance appreciation class was scheduled on the building's third floor. It also passed Resolution 1-25-S supporting 24/7 hours at The Commons at Helm Library during finals week, and Kurtz announced a POLLapalooza effort with a goal of 3,000 voters in the April election.

events.title: Resolution supported mental health advisory board
events.body: The Senate passed Resolution 4-25-S supporting the formation of a Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Advisory Board to advise upper-level administration on student mental health policy, with Dean of Students Martha Sales planned to oversee its creation. Co-author Emma Harris, the Resident Staff Association president, said Counseling Center staffing shortages had pushed students to rely on resident advisors. The Senate passed eight bills at the same meeting.

events.title: Senate voted to rename DEI Committee
events.body: Senators unanimously passed Bill 21-25-S, a constitutional amendment restructuring the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Committee and renaming it the Action and Opportunity Committee, following President Trump's executive order dismantling DEI mandates. The meeting initially lacked the 21 members needed for a two-thirds vote, so absent members were called onto Zoom to reach quorum. The amendment then went to a student referendum during the April 13-15 election.

events.title: Students ratified DEI amendment with 88% of vote
events.body: In the spring election, the student body approved Bill 21-25-S, the constitutional amendment renaming the DEI Committee to the Action and Opportunity Committee, with 88% of votes in favor. Committee chair Megan Farmer said the committee at its core was not changing and the rename was meant to better communicate its actions. Results for 31 senate seats were announced the same night.

events.title: 24th Senate held final meeting
events.body: The 24th Senate met for the last time on April 15 with no legislation on the agenda, spending the meeting on farewells. President Sam Kurtz, Vice President Donte Reed and Chief Financial Officer Ethan Taylor each received a standing ovation, and the Senate recorded 295 spring scholarship applications, far above the roughly 40-applicant average of past years.

events.title: 24th Senate installed: Vincent elected speaker, Henderson named chief justice
events.body: At the 24th Senate's first meeting, newly elected senators were sworn in and Sarah Vincent, College of Health and Human Services senator, was elected Speaker of the Senate over Sophia Bryant. Senior senator Anne-Marie Wright was appointed Chief of Staff, and Associate Chief Justice Ellen Henderson was appointed Chief Justice. Outgoing Chief Justice Isaac King swore in the new officers, officially opening the 2024-25 term.

events.title: Committee chairs and Judicial Council approved at fall opener
events.body: At the 24th Senate's first fall meeting, the Senate unanimously approved Kurtz's nominations of Aziz Umarov, Madison Payne, Neill Kane and Sam Dorris to the 2024-25 Judicial Council, and confirmed six committee chairs: Hannah Evans (Legislative Operations), Savanna Kurtz (Student Experience and Enrollment), Ryan Dilts (Outreach and Public Relations), Megan Farmer (DEI), Sophia Bryant (Student Mental Health and Wellbeing) and Annie Finch (Community Relations). President Timothy Caboni addressed the Senate on campus building renovations, the Mahurin Honors College restructuring and WKU's push for R2 research status.

events.title: Senate backs Myanmar flag, funds organizational aid and calculators
events.body: The Senate unanimously passed Resolution 5-24-F backing a Myanmar flag on the empty pole outside the Mahurin Honors College, sought by senators after students said Burmese and Chin students had no flag representing them; Bill 9-24-F distributed $10,000 in fall Organizational Aid funding across 58 graded applications; and Bill 10-24-F added $540 to buy five more calculators for the Borrow-a-Calculator program, which had lent 28 calculators that semester. Kurtz appointed freshman Emaun Riley as ISEC senator and Mahurin Honors College senator Caden Lucas as the Senate's parliamentarian.

leaders.name: Rush Robinson
leaders.note: Elected 13-15 April 2025 on a turnout of 966. Told the Faculty Senate to 'take a field trip' to see the state of WKU's residence halls. Handed his successor the red suit jacket on 28 April 2026.

sources.label: WKU News - Board of Regents, 8 Aug 2025

profile: Robinson, a senior from Benton, Kentucky triple-majoring in psychology, philosophy and sociology and a member of Sigma Phi Epsilon and Omicron Delta Kappa, won the SGA presidency in the 13-15 April 2025 general election on a turnout of 966, running with Savanna Kurtz for vice president and Gabriel Jerdon for chief financial officer. He also succeeded Sam Kurtz as WKU's student regent; the Board of Regents administered his oath of office on 8 August 2025, the same meeting at which it named the new Gordon Ford College of Business building Amy and David Chandler Hall and elected Jan West chair, Doris Thomas vice chair and Melissa Dennison secretary for 2025-26.

Robinson ran on turning SGA away from national politics and toward direct student advocacy, saying the organization had sometimes echoed national political talking points and that he wanted it to act as "an advocate and resource for students" who could be pointed to the right contact in the administration. His cabinet - Kurtz as vice president, Jerdon as chief financial officer, Maggie Yelton as chief of staff, and Preston Jenkins, reappointed chief communications officer on 22 April 2025 and confirmed by the Senate - ran a legislative program heavy on small, direct-benefit measures: vouchers for CPR certification, dental cleanings, transcripts and identification cards, equipment to borrow such as umbrellas, calculators and hammocks, and a resolution urging accessible restroom stalls in Grise Hall. Jenkins also organized a student-painted mural for a column in the SGA chambers. In March 2026 SGA drew on its projects fund to host a baseball-game tailgate, a response to Athletics Director Todd Stewart's call for more student engagement. The Senate closed its final meeting on 14 April 2026 having passed 56 bills for the year, the most since 2018-19, with Jenkins also reporting that a new university Artificial Intelligence Committee was weighing bulk AI-product subscriptions for students.

Robinson's most sustained policy push was on student mental health, working with Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee chair Veronica Butler on a year-long program backed by data from social work professor Jay Gabbard, who told SGA that 44 percent of WKU students reported depression symptoms and 10 percent had considered suicide in the past year. SGA co-organized Mental Health Week with the WKU Counseling Center and the campus NAMI chapter, ran a Toppers Talk About It awareness campaign, and had student recommendations - including relocating counseling services from Potter Hall to the Downing Student Union - reviewed by the Counseling Center Review Committee before forwarding them to administrators, though Butler said it was unclear whether they would be enacted. The push closed with an Out of Darkness suicide-remembrance walk on 18 April 2026, and successor Caden Lucas said the focus would continue "in a sustained and meaningful way."

At the Senate's first meeting under his successor, Robinson opened by telling the mostly-new chamber they looked untainted by SGA's usual troubles, then handed president-elect Caden Lucas the red suit jacket passed president to president - the same jacket Sam Kurtz had given him the year before. His term as student regent outlasted his SGA presidency: at the Board of Regents' 5 June 2026 meeting, his last as regent, he cast the lone vote against a $204, 1.69 percent tuition increase, saying the board had "to do whatever we can to not raise the tuition" to preserve affordability. Afterward he planned to remain at WKU for an Ed.S. in school psychology, aiming for a career as a school psychologist in a school district.

events.body: In one of his first acts after taking office, Robinson reappointed Preston Jenkins as chief communications officer; the Senate later confirmed the pick unanimously.

events.body: The Board of Regents administered Robinson's oath of office as student regent, succeeding graduating president Sam Kurtz. At the same meeting the board elected Jan West chair, Doris Thomas vice chair and Melissa Dennison secretary for 2025-26.

events.body: The new Gordon Ford College of Business building, named Amy and David Chandler Hall after a $7.5 million gift and funded largely by a Kentucky General Assembly appropriation, opened to students on the first day of fall classes.

events.title: SGA commissioned a student-painted mural for the chambers
events.body: Chief Communications Officer Preston Jenkins announced a plan to have four student artists each paint one side of a column in the SGA chambers, incorporating WKU campus elements, with selections due by 19 September.

events.title: Senate revived the transcript voucher program
events.body: The senate passed Bill 24-25-F, authored by Legislative Operations Committee Chair Caden Lucas, allocating $195 to reestablish the transcript voucher program, giving students one free official transcript a semester. It also funded a new "Professor of the Month" award and ping pong equipment for the DSU recreation area.

events.title: WKU Restaurant Group answered senators' questions
events.body: Restaurant Group representatives fielded senator questions on the removal of Steak 'n Shake seasoning, kiosks in Subway and adding spicy chicken sandwiches to Chick-fil-A's meal-swipe menu, and said the service handled about 60,000 meal transactions a week.

events.title: CPR-voucher bill and Grise Hall accessibility resolution passed
events.body: The senate unanimously passed Bill 2-26-S, funding six vouchers for free CPR certification, and Resolution 7-25-F, supporting additional handicapped-accessible restroom stalls in Grise Hall after a student's father said the building had only one large stall.

events.title: Senate adopted a fully codified rewrite of its bylaws
events.body: The Senate adopted an official codified version of the SGA Executive and Legislative Bylaws, superseding all prior versions, effective 24 February 2026.

events.title: Senate learns the Gilbane housing partnership cleared the legislature
events.body: At its Thursday meeting SGA senators learned that the Kentucky Legislature had approved WKU's public-private partnership with developer Gilbane, which the Board of Regents had provisionally approved 11 December 2025 to design and build a new residence hall replacing Douglas Keen and Hugh Poland Halls. "WKU is now in the clear to start building the new residence halls," said Senator Jakob Barker, who with Senator Ethan Vietze also sponsored Resolution 7-26-S, backing a crosswalk at Alumni Avenue and Kentucky Street for residents of the 1355 Kentucky Street apartments who Barker's resolution said had to "step into oncoming traffic" to reach the Alumni Square parking garage. The same meeting passed legislation funding textbooks, exam supplies and lab goggles and authorizing a student-experience survey.

events.title: SGA funded a tailgate to boost turnout at a baseball game
events.body: SGA used its projects fund to host free hot dogs, giveaways and a scholarship drawing before WKU baseball's home game against Louisville, an effort Robinson said answered Athletics Director Todd Stewart's call for more student engagement at games.

events.title: Weekly meeting funded a senior cookout, transfer cords and spikeball nets
events.body: SGA allocated $602.58 through three bills and a resolution: a senior sunset cookout, 240 transfer-student graduation cords, borrowable spikeball nets, and DSU signage improvements. CFO Gabriel Jerdon said the legislative discretionary fund would have $71.17 left if the following week's final bills all passed as written.

events.title: 25th Senate closes the year having passed 56 bills, the most since 2018-19
events.body: The 25th Senate's final meeting passed its last three bills of the year - funding an NPHC preview day, the Office of Sustainability's food pantry, and massage-therapy vouchers for finals week, the latter two amended to spend down the year's remaining $71.17 budget - bringing the year's total to 56 pieces of legislation. Chief Communications Officer Preston Jenkins reported that WKU's new Artificial Intelligence Committee, which he sat on, was in early talks about bulk subscriptions to AI products such as ChatGPT Pro for all students and a possible introductory AI course for freshmen. Guest speakers included a Parking and Transportation representative, who said the bus system's diesel bill had roughly doubled amid rising fuel prices. The Herald identified her as "Ginny Griffin"; the official senate minutes give her name as "Jenny Griffith" - unresolved which is correct.

events.title: Robinson cast the lone dissenting vote on a tuition increase
events.body: At his last meeting as student regent, Robinson voted against a $204, 1.69 percent tuition increase that the rest of the Board of Regents approved, saying the board had to do everything it could to preserve affordability.

events.title: Two tickets take questions in the DSU auditorium
events.body: Caden Lucas with Jakob Barker and Will Derryberry against Jaden Marshall with Kaden Blankenship and Miles VanRude. Chief Justice Sophie Stirling moderated questions submitted by the student body.

events.title: Turnout jumps 66% in a contested race
events.body: 1,601 students voted, 635 more than the year before. Lucas won. The clearest evidence in the whole record that WKU turnout tracks whether there is an actual contest.

events.title: Robinson tells the Faculty Senate to look at the dorms
events.body: Sitting next to Faculty Regent Shane Spiller during a discussion of WKU housing, Robinson told senators to 'take a field trip' and see the state of the residence halls.

events.title: The red suit jacket changes hands
events.body: At the first meeting of the 26th Senate, Robinson handed Lucas the red suit jacket, "the one that Sam (Kurtz) gave me." The same night, Gabby Pace, Cayden Bailey, Maggie Phelps and Jaden Marshall were sworn in to their new roles.

events.title: Year-long mental health push closed with the Out of Darkness Walk
events.body: Robinson and Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee chair Veronica Butler spent the year pressing WKU on student mental health, citing data from social work professor Jay Gabbard that 44 percent of students reported depression symptoms and 10 percent had considered suicide in the past year. SGA co-ran Mental Health Week with the WKU Counseling Center and campus NAMI chapter, launched a Toppers Talk About It campaign, and forwarded student recommendations - including moving counseling services out of Potter Hall - through the Counseling Center Review Committee. The year closed with an Out of Darkness suicide-remembrance walk on April 18; incoming president Caden Lucas said the focus would continue.

leaders.name: Caden Lucas
leaders.note: From Harned. Beat Jaden Marshall in a contested race on a turnout of 1,601 - up 66% on the previous year. WKU Spiritmaster, chair of the Hilltoppers Vote Coalition, works for the City of Bowling Green's Downtown Development Division. Sworn in 28 April 2026 at the first meeting of the 26th Senate.

sources.label: WKU News - ODK Circle Leader of the Year

profile: Lucas entered SGA in September 2024 as its inaugural student senator for the Mahurin Honors College, a seat created as the college began a program revision; he was also an Honors Teaching Fellow for HON 251, working with first-year Honors students on civic engagement. A junior senator, WKU Spiritmaster, chairman of the Hilltoppers Vote Coalition and an employee of Bowling Green's Downtown Development Division, he won the SGA presidential election on April 15, 2026, with running mates Jakob Barker for vice president and Will Derryberry for chief financial officer. Running under the motto "Lead, build, deliver," his campaign centered on increasing awareness of SGA operations and outreach to the student body, and he defeated Jaden Marshall, who had sought to become the first Black male student body president. After the results were announced Lucas said he felt "electric" and that the "work starts tomorrow," beginning with thank-you cards to supporters.

Lucas took office at the first meeting of the 26th Senate on April 28, 2026, where outgoing president Rush Robinson presented him with the traditional red suit jacket passed from president to president. Lucas thanked the new cabinet, nominated his defeated campaign opponent Jaden Marshall as an at-large senator, calling his campus work "phenomenal," and saw Gabi Pace and Cayden Bailey sworn in as chief of staff and chief communications officer. The meeting's speaker election deadlocked 9-9 between Amelia Tucker and Veronica Butler, a situation the governing documents did not address, and Butler won the seat in a re-vote.

Days after taking office, Lucas was named a 2026 Truman Scholar, WKU's second in the award's history and Kentucky's only recipient that year, chosen from 781 candidates nationally; the scholarship funds $30,000 toward graduate or professional study for students committed to public service. A political science, legal studies and strategic communications major, he had spent that summer establishing the Civic Engagement Resource Center, a joint Mahurin Honors College, SGA and Housing and Residence Life initiative that opened 30 October 2024 with a lending collection on civic life, saying his goal was to get students "talking about what it means to be a good citizen." In May, WKU's Omicron Delta Kappa circle named him its Heather Strode Circle Leader of the Year, an award recognizing collaboration, inclusivity, integrity, scholarship and service.

Before he was sworn in as student regent, Lucas told the Herald he was "generally concerned" by a proposed $210 tuition increase; the Board of Regents approved a $204 increase days later, with outgoing regent Rush Robinson casting the only dissenting vote before handing the seat to Lucas.
